stories.title: Sensex and Nifty look set for a higher open as softer US inflation and cooling oil prices lift sentiment
stories.what_happened: After Wednesday's **528.89-point (-0.68%) fall** in the Sensex to 77,625.36, and the Nifty's slide to roughly 24,307, Indian markets are positioned for a rebound today on the back of **softer-than-expected US inflation data**, gains in Wall Street technology stocks, and a pullback in crude oil. **Brent crude eased 1.2% to $87.9 a barrel** and US WTI fell 1.3% to $82.1, offering relief after days of oil-driven pressure tied to the Strait of Hormuz standoff between the US and Iran. The rupee had weakened to around **₹95.42 per dollar** amid the elevated crude prices and continued foreign institutional investor outflows. Positive cues from Asian markets overnight are reinforcing the improved sentiment heading into today's trading session.
key_points: Indian markets are positioned for a **positive open** today, helped by softer-than-feared **US inflation data** and gains on Wall Street tech stocks.
**Brent crude fell 1.2% to $87.9 a barrel**, and US WTI crude dropped 1.3% to $82.1 — easing one of the biggest recent drags on Indian stocks.
This follows a rough **Wednesday session**, when the Sensex fell **528.89 points (-0.68%)** to 77,625.36 and the Nifty slid to around 24,307.
The rupee had been trading near **₹95.42 to the dollar**, pressured by elevated crude prices and continued foreign-fund outflows.
Positive **Asian cues** overnight are adding to the improved mood heading into today's session.

depth.background: Indian equities have been under pressure for days from a mix of factors: rising crude oil prices tied to the **US-Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz**, a weakening rupee, and company-specific shocks like **Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran's abrupt resignation**, which dragged Tata group stocks and the wider Sensex lower earlier this week. Indian markets are highly sensitive to oil prices because India imports the vast majority of the crude it consumes, so even small moves in Brent crude quickly show up in the rupee and in import-heavy sectors.

stories.title: A new study finds the speed of global warming — not just its final level — decides whether a critical Atlantic current collapses
stories.what_happened: Researchers at **Utrecht University** ran climate simulations testing what happens to the AMOC under different warming speeds, not just different warming totals. They found that when CO2-driven warming happens **rapidly, the AMOC can collapse at around 2°C** of global warming — a threshold the world could cross within decades on current trends. But when the same amount of warming happens **slowly, the ocean has time to adapt**, and the current can stay stable even past **5°C**. The study, published in the journal **Nature Climate Change**, argues that the rate of change matters as much as the final temperature target. This matters directly for climate policy: many plans, including elements tied to the Paris Agreement, assume it's acceptable to temporarily 'overshoot' a temperature target as long as it's brought back down later — this research suggests that overshoot strategy could be far riskier than assumed if the overshoot happens fast.
key_points: Dutch researchers found that **rapid warming can collapse the AMOC current at just 2°C**, while slow warming lets it survive **past 5°C**.
The AMOC is the ocean current system that carries **warm tropical water north**, keeping Western Europe's climate mild.
The study, from **Utrecht University**, was published in **Nature Climate Change**.
It challenges climate policy built around **'overshoot' pathways** that assume peak warming can be temporary.
A collapsed AMOC would bring **much colder winters to Europe** and disrupt weather patterns worldwide.

depth.background: The **Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC)** is a system of ocean currents — including the Gulf Stream — that carries warm water from the tropics up toward Europe and the Arctic, then sends cooler, denser water back south at depth, like a giant conveyor belt. It's a major reason Western Europe is milder than other places at the same latitude (like parts of Canada). Scientists have warned for years that melting ice and warming oceans could weaken or even shut this system down, and past studies have disagreed on how close that tipping point actually is. This new research adds a twist: it's not just how hot the planet gets, but how fast it gets there, that determines whether the AMOC survives.

stories.title: China and Indonesia hold their first-ever joint navy drill east of Taiwan, and Taipei calls it a 'military provocation'
stories.what_happened: China's defence ministry said a Chinese warship and an Indonesian frigate conducted a 'passage exercise' in waters east of Taiwan in mid-August, describing it as meant to 'enhance the joint operational capabilities of the two navies' and 'jointly safeguard regional peace and stability.' It is the first time China has held a naval drill with a foreign military specifically in those waters. Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council strongly condemned the move, accusing Beijing of trying to create the false impression that China has jurisdiction over waters east of Taiwan and calling it a violation of Taiwan's sovereignty. Indonesia's navy pushed back on the framing, saying the exercise is a routine 'passing exercise' — a 'universal naval tradition' conducted while transiting another country's maritime area — as the Indonesian ship returned from a visit to Russia. Taipei Times reported the story as still developing as of August 13.
key_points: A **Chinese warship and an Indonesian frigate** are running a joint 'passage exercise' in waters **east of Taiwan** — the first time China has drilled with a foreign navy there.
Taiwan's China-policy body condemned it as **'CCP military provocation'**, saying it falsely implies China has jurisdiction over those waters.
Indonesia's navy says the drill is **routine**, calling it a standard 'passing exercise' on the way home from a port visit to **Russia**.
It's part of a broader pattern of China projecting military reach near Taiwan using **third-country partners**, not just its own fleet.

depth.background: Beijing claims Taiwan as its own territory and has spent years ramping up military pressure around the island — near-daily jet incursions, large-scale drills, and coast guard patrols meant to normalize a Chinese presence in disputed waters. Taiwan, a self-governing democracy of 23 million people, rejects that claim and is informally backed by the **United States**, which sells it weapons and has long signaled it would help defend the island if attacked. Indonesia is not a China ally in any formal sense — it's the world's largest Muslim-majority nation and usually prizes non-alignment — which is what makes this joint drill notable.

stories.title: BCCI seeks the Indian government's go-ahead before confirming a Bangladesh tour, as cricket ties stay strained
stories.what_happened: BCCI sources say the board has locked in a proposed window for a six-match tour of Bangladesh but will not confirm it until it receives formal approval from the Indian government — standard practice for tours to countries where diplomatic sensitivities are in play. This follows a visit by BCB president Tamim Iqbal to the BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru, which cricket officials on both sides described as a positive step toward normalizing relations. The tour, originally scheduled for August 2025, was deferred by mutual agreement to September 2026 after the earlier diplomatic rupture.
key_points: BCCI says it will approach the **Indian government** for formal clearance before confirming a tour of Bangladesh
Tensions began in **January 2026** when BCCI asked KKR to release Bangladeshi bowler Mustafizur Rahman from the IPL
Bangladesh's board (BCB) then **refused to travel to India** for the 2026 T20 World Cup, citing security advice
A recent visit by **BCB president Tamim Iqbal** to the BCCI's Bengaluru academy has revived hopes for the tour
The series was originally set for **August 2025** before being deferred to **September 2026**

depth.background: Cricket ties between India and Bangladesh soured amid the political turmoil in Bangladesh under its interim government led by Muhammad Yunus, feeding into a broader chill in bilateral relations. The flashpoint came when BCCI, citing violence against religious minorities in Bangladesh, asked Kolkata Knight Riders to release Bangladeshi pace bowler Mustafizur Rahman from their IPL 2026 squad — a request Bangladesh's board answered days later by pulling its national team out of traveling to India for the 2026 T20 World Cup over security concerns. Since then, ties have shown signs of thawing under new Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

stories.title: Red Bull says fixing car 'consistency' — not a big upgrade — is the key to its second-half fightback
stories.what_happened: Red Bull team principal **Laurent Mekies** said the RB22's central weakness this season has been a lack of **consistency** rather than a lack of outright pace — the car is unusually sensitive to small variables like kerb strikes, gravel pickup, or changing wind direction, which has repeatedly undermined driver confidence lap to lap. Mekies said fixing that sensitivity, to reliably hand Max Verstappen and teammate Isack Hadjar a car they can trust, is where he sees the most available performance gain for the second half of 2026, rather than pursuing a major new aerodynamic package. His comments echo Verstappen's own description of the car showing unusual **'car degradation'** through races.
key_points: Team boss **Laurent Mekies** says the RB22's core issue is **inconsistency**, not raw pace.
Small factors — kerb damage, wind direction — have been knocking driver confidence in the car all season.
Verstappen has separately flagged **'car degradation'** as a specific concern with the RB22.
Red Bull is targeting **balance and qualifying gains**, not a headline aerodynamic overhaul, for the second half.

depth.background: Formula 1 teams get limited in-season upgrade budget under the sport's cost cap, so identifying the *right* problem to fix matters as much as having the resources to fix it. Red Bull's RB22, built for F1's new 2026 technical rules, has shown flashes of competitive pace this season but has struggled to deliver it reliably from session to session — a very different problem from simply lacking downforce or power. Max Verstappen has been racing this car while also facing swirling questions about his contract and future at the team.

stories.title: Ferrari's real problem isn't downforce — it's rear-tyre management, data shows
stories.what_happened: Ferrari engineers concluded, after comparing data from the **Red Bull Ring and Silverstone**, that the SF-26's real limitation is **inconsistent rear-tyre behaviour and management**, not simply insufficient downforce as had been assumed. In response, Ferrari is bringing an **evolved floor** to the **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort** (August 21-23) — an update on the floor first introduced in Barcelona — designed to improve downforce and stability specifically through Zandvoort's fast, banked, flowing corners, which put a premium on exactly the kind of balance Ferrari has lacked. This is the first of three planned upgrade steps: the Zandvoort floor, an **ADUO-2 engine upgrade worth roughly +15 horsepower at Monza**, and further changes expected by the Austin race. The update comes after a mixed Hungarian Grand Prix in which Charles Leclerc qualified 2nd but finished 4th, over 23 seconds behind the winner.
key_points: A technical analysis of Ferrari's **SF-26** after the Hungarian Grand Prix found its main weakness is **rear-tyre management**, not a lack of downforce.
Ferrari is bringing an **evolved floor** — built on the version introduced in Barcelona — to the **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort**.
Zandvoort's fast, banked corners make it a strong track to test whether the new floor genuinely fixes the car's balance over a full lap.
The floor update is step one of a **three-race development plan**: Zandvoort (floor), **Monza (ADUO-2 engine upgrade, +15hp)**, then Austin.
Leclerc has shown flashes of pace but slipped from **2nd on the grid to 4th** in Hungary, finishing over 23 seconds behind the race winner.

depth.background: Formula 1 cars are re-engineered constantly through a season via **upgrade packages** — new floors, wings and engine tweaks — as teams chase performance within strict cost and testing limits. Ferrari has spent 2026 chasing **Mercedes and McLaren** for the constructors' title, with a car that has a strong chassis and braking but has struggled to convert single-lap pace into race results. Engineers compare data from multiple circuits (in this case the Red Bull Ring and Silverstone) to diagnose exactly what's limiting a car's performance before committing to expensive new parts.

stories.title: ISRO launches AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird Block-2 — the heaviest satellite ever lifted from Indian soil
stories.what_happened: ISRO successfully launched the BlueBird Block-2 communication satellite on its LVM3-M6 rocket from Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, at 8:55 AM IST. After a flight of about 15 minutes, the satellite separated from the rocket and was placed into its intended orbit. ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan called it the heaviest satellite ever lifted off Indian soil by an Indian launch vehicle. The mission is part of AST SpaceMobile's global low-Earth-orbit constellation, which aims to provide direct-to-mobile satellite connectivity to ordinary phones.
key_points: ISRO launched the **BlueBird Block-2** satellite on its heaviest rocket, the **LVM3-M6**, from Sriharikota at **8:55 AM IST**.
ISRO's chairman called it the **heaviest satellite ever lifted from Indian soil** using an Indian-built launcher.
The satellite separated and reached orbit after a roughly **15-minute flight**.
It's part of **AST SpaceMobile's** global constellation for **direct-to-mobile** connectivity — letting ordinary smartphones connect to satellites without special hardware.

depth.background: LVM3 (formerly known as GSLV Mk III) is ISRO's most powerful operational rocket, built to carry India's heaviest payloads and increasingly used to launch other countries' commercial satellites for a fee. AST SpaceMobile is a US company building a constellation of large low-Earth-orbit satellites designed to connect directly to regular, unmodified smartphones — filling in cellular 'dead zones' without needing special satellite phones. India's space program has been steadily building a commercial launch business alongside its own missions, competing for a slice of the growing global demand for satellite launches.

stories.title: Jharkhand police file cases against 600 protesters after violent clashes at recruitment-exam demonstration
stories.what_happened: Jharkhand Police have registered FIRs against roughly 600 people over alleged violence during the August 10 march on the Assembly, naming 100 individuals directly and booking another 500 as unidentified. Student leader Devendra Nath Mahto, who was leading the demonstration, was among those detained by police, who used lathi charges, tear gas shells and water cannons to break up the crowd. Investigators say they are reviewing video footage, CCTV recordings and drone camera footage from the protest site, and have signaled that facial-recognition and AI-based identification technology may be used if needed to identify additional suspects. The police action has spilled into state politics: opposition BJP MLAs disrupted assembly proceedings over the crackdown, forcing the Speaker to adjourn the House twice.
key_points: Jharkhand Police have booked **600 protesters** — **100 named, 500 unidentified** — over violence during an Assembly 'gherao' march in Ranchi on August 10.
The protest is over alleged **irregularities and paper leaks** in JPSC and JSSC recruitment exams, now in its **20th day** of agitation.
Police used **lathi charges, tear gas and water cannons** to disperse the march; student leader Devendra Nath Mahto was detained.
Investigators are examining video, CCTV and drone footage, and may use **facial-recognition and AI-based tools** to identify protesters.
The crackdown forced Jharkhand's Assembly Speaker to **adjourn the House twice** after BJP MLAs protested the police action.

depth.background: For nearly three weeks, students and job aspirants have been protesting alleged irregularities in exams run by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC) — the state bodies that conduct recruitment tests for government jobs. Their core demand is an independent probe, ideally by the CBI or a panel of retired High Court judges from outside Jharkhand, into alleged paper leaks and irregularities, along with cancellation of the affected exams. The protests escalated on August 10 into a march to gherao (surround) the state Legislative Assembly in Ranchi.

stories.title: Oscar Piastri opens up on a rough title defence: 'more lows than highs' as rivals and pundits dissect his 2026 slump
stories.what_happened: Speaking during the summer break, Piastri admitted that his 2026 campaign has brought **'more lows than highs,'** acknowledging that both he and McLaren have fallen short of where they expected to be. He currently sits **sixth in the drivers' championship**, some 36 points behind teammate Lando Norris, even though Piastri still leads their head-to-head race record 5 wins to 4. McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said Piastri's natural, settled driving style has struggled to adapt to a 2026 car that rewards drivers willing to let the car move more aggressively through corners. Former McLaren driver Juan Pablo Montoya went further, suggesting the manner of Piastri's 2025 title loss may still be affecting his confidence. Piastri himself says he only worked out how to properly drive the 2026 car in the last few races before the summer break, and is hoping the second half of the season brings a turnaround.
key_points: Piastri admits his 2026 season has had **'more lows than highs'**, sitting sixth in the standings at the summer break.
He trails McLaren teammate **Lando Norris by 36 points**, despite leading their head-to-head in race wins 5-4.
McLaren boss **Andrea Stella** says Piastri's naturally smooth driving style is clashing with a 2026 car that rewards a more aggressive approach.
Ex-F1 driver **Juan Pablo Montoya** suggests the psychological hangover from **narrowly losing the 2025 title** may be playing a role in the dip.
Piastri says he's only recently 'discovered' how the 2026 car needs to be driven, and hopes for a stronger second half.

depth.background: Oscar Piastri came into 2026 as McLaren's reigning championship contender after a closely fought battle for the 2025 Drivers' title, which he ultimately lost. Formula 1 introduced a **new set of technical regulations for the 2026 season** — new car designs, engines and aerodynamic rules — which reset the competitive order and forced every driver to adapt to unfamiliar machinery. Piastri is known for a smooth, minimal-movement driving style that suited last year's cars, while teammate Norris has adapted more quickly to what the new-generation McLaren demands this season.

stories.title: Juan Pablo Montoya predicts Lance Stroll could walk away from his own father's F1 team if the car doesn't improve
stories.what_happened: Former F1 driver **Juan Pablo Montoya** said he expects **Lance Stroll to leave Aston Martin** if the team's car performance doesn't improve, telling reporters **'Stroll will leave if the car doesn't improve.'** Montoya argued that if Aston Martin isn't competitive next year, the team could have **two free seats in 2028** — both Stroll's and Alonso's. He noted Stroll is technically contracted for **2027 and beyond**, and is the son of team owner Lawrence Stroll, which usually protects his seat regardless of results. But Montoya's view is that even that protection has limits: at some point, still running at the back of the field could push Stroll himself to walk away. Asked directly about his future beyond this season while in Monaco, Stroll **declined to confirm** he'd still be racing in F1 next year, saying only that he was focused on the present.
key_points: Former F1 driver **Juan Pablo Montoya** predicts Lance Stroll will leave Aston Martin **if the car doesn't improve**.
Stroll's father, **Lawrence Stroll**, is Aston Martin's owner — making this a prediction about a driver leaving his own family's team.
Montoya says Aston Martin could have **two free seats in 2028** if performance doesn't pick up, since Alonso's future is also uncertain.
Stroll is contracted through **2027 and beyond**, but declined to confirm his plans when asked directly in Monaco.
The prediction lands the same week Aston Martin **fired team boss Graeme Lowdon**, adding to questions about the team's direction.

depth.background: **Lance Stroll** races for Aston Martin, the team owned by his father, billionaire **Lawrence Stroll** — a well-known dynamic in F1, since most drivers' seats depend purely on performance while Stroll's is also tied to family ownership. Aston Martin has struggled to match its ambitions this season despite big investment, and has been racing near the back of the field. Teammate **Fernando Alonso**'s own future with the team beyond 2027 has also been an open question, with rumors already swirling that Aston Martin could target Carlos Sainz as a replacement if Alonso leaves.

stories.title: Mitchell Starc becomes Test cricket's most successful left-arm bowler ever, passing Rangana Herath
stories.what_happened: During day two of the Australia-Bangladesh Test in Darwin, Mitchell Starc dismissed opener Shadman Islam to take his **434th Test wicket**, moving past Rangana Herath's **433** to become the leading left-arm bowler in Test cricket history. The milestone arrived in Starc's **106th Test appearance** and, fittingly, on **International Left-Handers Day**. The achievement also puts him level with India great **Kapil Dev** on the all-time wicket-takers list, and within six wickets of South Africa's **Dale Steyn (439)** for a place in the game's top ten leading wicket-takers overall, regardless of arm or bowling style.
key_points: Starc reached **434 Test wickets**, passing Sri Lanka's **Rangana Herath (433)** to become the most successful left-arm bowler in Test history.
He got there by dismissing Bangladesh opener **Shadman Islam** during the historic **Darwin Test**.
The milestone came in his **106th Test**, and fell on **International Left-Handers Day** (August 13).
Starc is now **level with Kapil Dev** on the all-time wicket-takers list, and just **six behind Dale Steyn's 439** for the top ten overall.

depth.background: Mitchell Starc has been Australia's frontline left-arm fast bowler for over a decade, known for swinging the new ball and reverse-swinging the old one. Left-arm bowlers face a quirk regardless of pace or style: there have simply been far fewer of them across cricket history than right-arm bowlers, which makes elite career wicket tallies rarer among them. Sri Lankan left-arm spinner **Rangana Herath** had held the left-arm wicket-taking record with 433 dismissals since his retirement. Starc reached the milestone during Australia's landmark first-ever home Test against Bangladesh, a fixture Bangladesh waited 23 years to secure.

stories.title: Jon Jones apologizes to Lewis Hamilton, five years after Hamilton called him a 'coward' and blocked him
stories.what_happened: Jon Jones revealed in a recent interview that Lewis Hamilton sent him **'a long message'** on social media in 2021, branding him **'a coward'** for shooting the pig, before unfollowing and blocking him. Jones said the reaction stung because he considered himself a genuine fan of Hamilton's — **'I was a fan of him, but he was very disappointed in me for shooting the pig,'** he said. In the years since, Jones has come to acknowledge the incident was wrong, and has now issued what's described as a heartfelt apology to Hamilton for his conduct. The story broke as Hamilton, now 41 and sitting second in the 2026 F1 championship standings, uses the sport's summer break to train ahead of the season's return at the Dutch Grand Prix in Zandvoort later this month.
key_points: UFC champion **Jon Jones** has apologized to Lewis Hamilton, five years after the F1 star cut him off over an animal-cruelty controversy
Hamilton, a longtime **animal-rights campaigner**, called Jones a **'coward'** and blocked him on social media back in **January 2021**
The falling-out followed a video of Jones **shooting a pig from a helicopter**, which went viral at the time
Jones revealed Hamilton sent him a long, angry message before unfollowing and blocking him — and says he was genuinely a fan hurt by the reaction
The story resurfaces as Hamilton, second in the F1 championship, prepares for the season's resumption at **Zandvoort** after the summer break

depth.background: **Lewis Hamilton** is a seven-time Formula 1 world champion and one of the sport's most outspoken advocates for animal welfare and environmental causes off the track. Back in **January 2021**, UFC heavyweight champion **Jon Jones** posted a video of himself shooting a pig from a helicopter, which drew immediate backlash online. Hamilton, who follows and is followed by many athletes across sports, reacted strongly at the time — sending Jones a pointed message, calling him a coward, and cutting off contact. The incident had largely faded from public view until Jones brought it up again recently.

stories.title: RBI turns notably more upbeat on India's economy as the worst-feared damage from the Iran war fails to materialize
stories.what_happened: India's central bank sounded **notably more confident** about the economy in its latest monthly report, five months after the Iran war first raised fears of an inflation spike and a broader slowdown. The **Monetary Policy Committee**, a six-member panel that sets interest rates, voted **unanimously** to hold the repo rate at **5.25%** for a **fourth consecutive meeting**, predicting inflation will ease further while growth stays resilient. The report points to concrete strength in demand: **vehicle sales at record levels**, **credit growth at a two-year high**, and **GST (India's national goods-and-services tax) receipts rising at a double-digit pace**. Inflation did pick up slightly last month, but it remained comfortably inside RBI's official **2%–6% tolerance band**. RBI's report still flags two live risks — the **unresolved Iran war** (which could yet push energy prices higher) and a **deficient monsoon**, since weak rains hurt farm output and rural spending.
key_points: RBI held its benchmark **repo rate at 5.25%** for a **fourth straight meeting**, with all six policy committee members voting to hold.
Vehicle sales are at **record levels**, credit growth has hit a **two-year high**, and **GST receipts are rising at a double-digit pace**.
Inflation ticked up slightly last month but stayed **inside RBI's 2%–6% comfort band**.
Five months ago, the Iran war had raised fears of an **inflation spike and downturn** in India — those fears have **'so far failed to materialize.'**
RBI still flags the **ongoing Iran war and a deficient monsoon** as risks to watch.

depth.background: The **repo rate** is the interest rate at which India's central bank, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, lends to commercial banks — it's the main lever RBI uses to control inflation and growth: raise it to cool the economy, cut it to stimulate. When the Iran-Israel-US war broke out roughly five months ago, it pushed global oil prices higher and unsettled markets, since India imports most of its oil and a spike in crude prices usually feeds directly into inflation and India's import bill. RBI, headed by Governor **Sanjay Malhotra**, has been watching that risk closely in its monthly economic reports ever since.

stories.title: L&T wins a $1.57 billion order to build India's biggest AI data centre, in a bet on the global AI compute boom
stories.what_happened: **Larsen & Toubro** announced on **August 13, 2026** that it secured an order worth up to **$1.57 billion** from **Together AI**, a US-based AI cloud platform, to build and host an AI data centre in **Chennai**. The facility, run through L&T's new AI-infrastructure arm **LTN Compute** at its Vyoma.AI campus, will house **10,000 Nvidia B300 chips** — the largest such deployment announced in India to date. It will support Together AI's cloud platform for AI training, fine-tuning and inference. L&T shares rose as much as **1.2%** in trading following the announcement.
key_points: **Larsen & Toubro** won an order worth up to **$1.57 billion (₹150 billion)** from US cloud firm **Together AI**.
The data centre will run **10,000 Nvidia B300 chips** — the largest such AI chip deployment in India.
It will be built at L&T's **Vyoma.AI** campus in **Chennai**, through its new AI-infrastructure arm **LTN Compute**.
L&T's stock rose as much as **1.2%** on the news.
It marks L&T's entry into the **'AI factory' business** — building physical infrastructure for AI, not just software.

depth.background: India has spent the past year courting AI data-centre investment — including a separate deal for L&T's Vyoma unit to build a facility in Gujarat's Dholera region. Globally, Big Tech's AI infrastructure commitments are approaching **$1.5 trillion**, and countries are racing to host a share of that build-out, competing on cheap power, land and engineering talent against hubs like the Gulf states and Southeast Asia. Nvidia's B300 chip is its newest AI accelerator, in short supply worldwide as AI labs race to lock in compute capacity.

stories.title: India's injury crunch deepens: Sai Sudharsan ruled out of the Sri Lanka Tests with a toe fracture, and captain Shubman Gill is now under an injury cloud too
stories.what_happened: India batter **Sai Sudharsan** has been ruled out of the upcoming two-Test series in Sri Lanka because of a **toe stress fracture** that hasn't healed enough for him to be declared fit. He had been named in the initial 15-man squad, but his selection — like Bumrah's — was conditional on medical clearance from the BCCI's Centre of Excellence, and he ultimately failed to get it in time; he did not travel with the squad and **no replacement has been named yet**. Adding to India's pre-series injury concerns, Test captain **Shubman Gill** is now also under an injury cloud after hurting his **right ring finger** during a training session in Colombo — a new issue, separate from an earlier finger problem that had already been reported resolved. The two-Test series begins **August 15 in Galle**, with the second Test starting **August 23** at the SSC in Colombo.
key_points: **Sai Sudharsan** is ruled out of the two-Test Sri Lanka series with a **toe stress fracture**.
He had been given a conditional spot pending fitness clearance from the BCCI's **Centre of Excellence (CoE)** — he didn't recover in time.
No replacement for Sudharsan has been named yet, and he did not travel with the squad to Sri Lanka.
Captain **Shubman Gill** is now also under an injury cloud after hurting his **right ring finger** in a training session in Colombo.
The series starts **August 15 in Galle**, with the second Test in **Colombo from August 23**.

depth.background: India named its Test squad for the Sri Lanka tour with some fitness question marks already attached: Sudharsan and Bumrah's places were both conditional on medical clearance after recent injuries, and Bumrah ultimately missed out. Sudharsan picked up a **toe stress fracture** — a small crack in the bone from repeated stress rather than a single impact — after returning from India A's tour of Sri Lanka in July, and had been at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence trying to recover in time.

thread.previously: When India named its 15-man Test squad for Sri Lanka, Jadeja returned from injury but Jasprit Bumrah was ruled out; Sai Sudharsan and Bumrah's spots had been made conditional on fitness clearance, and Gill's own earlier finger injury was reported as resolved.
thread.changed: Sudharsan has now failed that fitness test and is officially ruled out with a toe stress fracture, with no replacement yet named — and captain Shubman Gill has picked up a new, separate injury, hurting his right ring finger in training in Colombo just before the series starts.

stories.title: Astronomers using the James Webb telescope find a brand-new kind of cosmic object: a 'black hole star'
stories.what_happened: MIT-led astronomers spotted an unusually bright red dot in one of the deepest images JWST has ever taken, dating to just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang. The object looked like an enormous star — physically about the size of our solar system — but was radiating **100 billion times more energy** than any known star could physically generate. After ruling out other explanations, the team concluded the most likely answer is a hybrid never seen before: a **black hole embedded inside a giant envelope of hydrogen gas**, acting almost like the black hole is 'wearing' a star. They estimate the black hole at its centre is about **100,000 times the mass of the Sun**. The team has named the object MoM-BH*-1 and published the analysis in Nature. If the interpretation holds up under further observation, it would be the first confirmed example of an entirely new astrophysical category.
key_points: A team led by MIT found an object glowing with **100 billion times** more energy than any known star can produce.
It's a **supermassive black hole** (about 100,000 times the Sun's mass) wrapped in a hydrogen envelope roughly the size of our solar system.
Spotted by the **James Webb Space Telescope** just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang — one of the earliest objects ever seen.
Nicknamed **'MoM-BH*-1'**, it could explain how supermassive black holes grew so fast in the universe's infancy.
The findings were published in the journal **Nature**, and the team calls it a genuinely new class of object.

depth.background: Astronomers have long been puzzled by how **supermassive black holes** — the kind that sit at the centre of galaxies, including our own — managed to grow so enormous so quickly after the Big Bang. Normal black hole growth, where a black hole slowly swallows nearby gas and stars, is thought to be too slow to explain black holes this size existing only a few hundred million years into the universe's 13.8-billion-year history. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, was built partly to peer further back in time than any previous telescope, letting scientists directly observe this early era for the first time. Its 'Mirage or Miracle' survey — designed to hunt for exactly these kinds of puzzling early-universe objects — is what turned up this find.

stories.title: Delhi locks down central roads for Independence Day's full-dress rehearsal, with facial-recognition CCTV and a drone ban in force
stories.what_happened: Delhi Traffic Police closed multiple roads around **Red Fort** — including Netaji Subhash Marg, Lothian Road and S.P. Mukherjee Marg — from **4 am to 10 am** on August 13 for the full-dress rehearsal of the Independence Day ceremony, with only vehicles carrying valid rehearsal passes permitted through. The rehearsal tests the exact security setup planned for August 15: an estimated **15,000 to 20,000 police and paramilitary personnel**, about **1,000 CCTV cameras equipped with facial recognition**, and intensified checks by the Central Industrial Security Force that will continue through August 16. A citywide ban on drones, UAVs, paragliders, hot-air balloons and quadcopters has been in force since August 2 and runs until August 16 for the same reason. This year's ceremony theme is **'150 Years of Vande Mataram'** and **'Yuva Shakti for Viksit Bharat@2047'**.
key_points: Roads around **Red Fort** — including Netaji Subhash Marg and S.P. Mukherjee Marg — were closed from **4 am to 10 am** for today's rehearsal.
Security for the real event includes **15,000–20,000 police and paramilitary personnel** and roughly **1,000 facial-recognition CCTV cameras**.
**Drones, paragliders, hot-air balloons and quadcopters** are banned across Delhi from August 2 to August 16.
This year's theme marks **'150 Years of Vande Mataram'** and **'Yuva Shakti for Viksit Bharat@2047'**.
The rehearsal is the final security dry-run before PM Modi's **80th Independence Day** address on August 15.

depth.background: India's Parliament recently passed a law criminalizing disruption of Vande Mataram performances, clearing the way for this year's Independence Day ceremony to open with the national song at Red Fort for the first time in its history — a symbolic first tied to the song's 150th anniversary. Every year's Red Fort ceremony requires a full security rehearsal days ahead of the actual event, given the scale of the gathering, the VVIP presence of the Prime Minister, and Delhi's history as a target for security threats around the occasion.

thread.previously: We reported that Parliament had passed the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026, meaning this year's 80th Independence Day ceremony would open with Vande Mataram performed at Red Fort for the first time ever, before PM Modi's address — with disrupting the song now punishable by up to 3 years in prison.
thread.changed: Delhi held the full **dress rehearsal** for that ceremony today, shutting down major roads around Red Fort from **4 am to 10 am** and deploying the security apparatus that will be in place on August 15: **15,000–20,000 police and paramilitary personnel**, roughly **1,000 CCTV cameras with facial recognition**, and a citywide ban on drones, paragliders and other aerial devices running from August 2–16.

stories.title: Karnataka shuts down for a 12-hour bandh today over the Cauvery water dispute
stories.what_happened: The **Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA)** upheld an earlier order from the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee directing Karnataka to release **3,500 cusecs of water to Tamil Nadu for 15 days**. In response, Nagaraj called a **12-hour, statewide bandh for August 13**, also demanding movement on Karnataka's own long-pending water projects — **Mekedatu, Mahadayi, and Kalasa-Banduri**. Organisers say more than 2,000 organisations are backing the shutdown, including transport unions and traders' bodies in Bengaluru and Mysuru. CM Shivakumar asked Nagaraj to withdraw the call, warning of disruption, but Nagaraj rejected the appeal and confirmed preparations would continue.
key_points: Pro-Kannada groups led by veteran activist **Vatal Nagaraj** called a statewide bandh for **6am–6pm today**, backed by over **2,000 organisations**.
The trigger: a tribunal upheld an order for Karnataka to release **3,500 cusecs of Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu for 15 days**.
Karnataka's Chief Minister **D.K. Shivakumar** publicly appealed to Nagaraj to call it off — the appeal was **rejected**.
Schools, offices and essential services are expected to stay open, but **public transport, shops, and inter-state travel** face disruption.

depth.background: The Cauvery river dispute is one of India's longest-running inter-state conflicts: Karnataka and Tamil Nadu have fought for decades over how much water from the Cauvery (which originates in Karnataka) must be released downstream to Tamil Nadu, especially during dry spells. A series of tribunals and Supreme Court rulings have set sharing formulas, but each new release order still triggers protest in Karnataka, where farmers and Kannada activists see it as prioritising another state's needs over their own. Vatal Nagaraj has led such bandhs (shutdown protests) over the issue for years.

stories.title: India's Supreme Court accuses its food safety regulator of stalling on sugar-and-salt warning labels to protect industry
stories.what_happened: At a hearing on **August 13, 2026**, the Supreme Court sharply criticized FSSAI for failing to implement front-of-pack warning labels on packaged foods high in sugar, saturated fat or sodium, despite a **February 2026** court order giving it four weeks to finalize the framework. The bench asked whether FSSAI's inaction reflected pressure from food manufacturers, after the regulator disclosed that a **March 19, 2026** stakeholder consultation found most industry participants opposed warning labels, preferring a softer, non-alarming information system instead. FSSAI's own draft proposal calls for pictorial labels flagging products exceeding **25 grams of sugar, 10 grams of saturated fat, or 5 grams of salt** per recommended daily limit.
key_points: The Supreme Court asked **FSSAI**, India's food regulator, **'Do you not want people to be healthy?'** over its delay on warning labels.
FSSAI was ordered in **February 2026** to finalize front-of-pack warning labels within four weeks — and still hasn't.
A **March 2026** industry consultation found most food companies **opposed** mandatory warning labels.
The court directly asked whether FSSAI's inaction reflects **pressure from food manufacturers**.
The proposed labels would flag foods exceeding **25g sugar, 10g saturated fat, or 5g salt** per recommended daily limits.

depth.background: India is facing a fast-rising burden of diabetes, obesity and heart disease, and health advocates have pushed for years for mandatory front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food — similar to rules already in force in Chile, Mexico and the UK, which use warning symbols to flag products high in sugar, fat or salt. FSSAI's proposed labels are based on daily limits set out in the **2024 ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians**. The regulator has repeatedly missed its own deadlines to finalize the rule, most recently one the Supreme Court set in February 2026.

stories.title: Treasury Secretary Bessent vows 'economic isolation' of Iran unlike anything seen before, with details due next week
stories.what_happened: Speaking to Newsmax's 'Rob Schmitt Tonight' on the evening of **August 13**, Bessent said: **'Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of the economic isolation of a country.'** He described the coming plan as **'a combination of economic isolation like the world has never seen before, and the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz that will keep anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports.'** He did not detail what the specific new measures would be, only that they are still being finalized. The comments confirm that Washington's strategy going forward leans on financial and trade pressure rather than a wider bombing campaign.
key_points: Bessent says the US will apply sanctions **'like have never been seen'** in the history of isolating a country.
New measures are due to be announced **'next week.'**
The plan pairs new sanctions with the **continued naval blockade** of Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz.
It signals the US is leaning on **economic pressure instead of an all-out bombing campaign** against Tehran.
Bessent has already issued a **series of sanctions** on Iranian figures and proxies over the past year.

depth.background: The US has been at war with Iran for roughly six months, largely fought through air power, a naval blockade, and sanctions rather than a ground invasion. Treasury Secretary **Scott Bessent** has been the point person for the sanctions side of that campaign, repeatedly targeting Iranian officials, front companies, and militia proxies funded by Tehran. His comments this week suggest the administration is preparing to escalate that economic track sharply, even as the military side — carrier deployments, the Hormuz blockade — continues in parallel.

stories.title: Ex-Ferrari engineer Rob Smedley says Haas will 'never' be F1 frontrunners under its current ownership model
stories.what_happened: Rob Smedley argued on the High Performance Racing podcast that Haas's current business structure permanently caps its competitive ceiling, saying the team **'will never have the possibility of being frontrunners'** as long as it stays organized the way it is. His comments echoed criticism from broadcaster Jake Humphrey, who called Haas 'the team I find the most frustrating on the grid' for repeatedly starting a season with a fast car and then failing to develop it further, questioning whether the team simply lacks the resources or technical depth to keep improving. As of the mid-season point, Haas sits **seventh in the constructors' championship with 21 points**, with drivers Oliver Bearman (18 points, 13th) and Esteban Ocon (3 points, 17th) both well off the leading pace.
key_points: Rob Smedley, a former Ferrari race engineer, said Haas **'will never have the possibility of being frontrunners'** under its current team structure.
He made the comments on the **High Performance Racing podcast**, offering a blunt mid-season verdict on the team.
Haas currently sits **7th in the constructors' championship with 21 points**, with drivers Oliver Bearman (13th) and Esteban Ocon (17th).
Broadcaster **Jake Humphrey** separately criticized Haas for repeatedly starting seasons fast but failing to develop the car.
The critique centers on Haas's **lean business model** — it doesn't own a full factory the way rival teams do — limiting how much it can invest in upgrades.

depth.background: **Haas** is F1's smallest and leanest team, historically outsourcing much of its car design and manufacturing to partners (Ferrari for the power unit and some parts, Dallara for chassis production) rather than building a full in-house factory like Red Bull, Mercedes, or Ferrari. This model keeps costs down but has long been criticized as a structural ceiling on how competitive Haas can become, since it can't develop upgrades at the same pace as bigger-budget rivals. Haas has flashed promise in the past — starting seasons with a fast car — but has repeatedly faded as the season wears on and competitors out-develop it. **Rob Smedley** is a respected F1 figure, having spent years as a senior race engineer and strategist at Ferrall and Williams before moving into broadcasting and commentary.

stories.title: Red Bull's mid-season report card: a car that's hard to tame, and an engine locked out of upgrades under F1's new rules
stories.what_happened: Mid-season assessments of the 2026 F1 grid describe Red Bull as a team that started the year as only the fourth-fastest, hampered by a car that's difficult to set up and keep in its performance window — both Max Verstappen and rookie teammate Isack Hadjar have battled unpredictable handling at most events. Compounding the issue, F1's engine regulations have effectively frozen the current benchmark power unit design, meaning Red Bull-Ford Powertrains can no longer add meaningful upgrades to their new in-house engine even if it's behind rivals. Despite this, the team has thrown a large number of aerodynamic upgrades at its RB22 chassis and clawed back significant pace — Verstappen has taken four podium finishes this season, three of them in the last four races, even though he hasn't yet won a race in 2026. The ongoing car issues have, predictably, reignited speculation about Verstappen's long-term future at the team.
key_points: Red Bull started 2026 as the **fourth-fastest team**, struggling with poor starts and a car that's hard to set up.
Both Verstappen and teammate **Isack Hadjar** have suffered unpredictable handling at most races this year.
F1's V6 engine rules mean the **benchmark power unit is now frozen**, effectively locking Red Bull-Ford Powertrains out of further upgrades to it.
Despite the struggles, Red Bull has clawed back pace with heavy **aerodynamic upgrades**, and Verstappen has taken **four podiums**, three in the last four races.
The car troubles have reignited the now-annual round of **Verstappen future speculation**.

depth.background: 2026 marked a major regulation shift in F1, with new engine rules that let teams design their own power units — Red Bull built its own in-house 'Red Bull-Ford Powertrains' unit for the first time, a significant technical gamble. Early in the season Red Bull was over a second off the pace in Australia, a stark contrast to its recent championship dominance.

stories.title: Verstappen says Alonso 'deserves to be top five, not P21' as Cadillac moves to shut down Perez-to-Williams rumours
stories.what_happened: In comments this week, Max Verstappen weighed in on Fernando Alonso's difficult season, saying Alonso 'doesn't deserve to be P21' and 'deserves to be in the top five, minimum' — a pointed remark on the gap between Alonso's talent and Aston Martin's current competitiveness. The comments add fuel to speculation about whether Alonso, out of contract concerns, could look to leave the team. Separately, Cadillac's senior leadership pushed back on reports suggesting Sergio Perez, one of two veteran drivers signed for the team's debut season, could depart for Williams at the end of 2026, insisting he remains part of their plans.
key_points: Max Verstappen said **'Fernando doesn't deserve to be P21. Fernando deserves to be in the top five, minimum'** about Alonso's struggling Aston Martin campaign.
The comments fuel ongoing **'silly season'** speculation about whether Alonso could seek a way out of Aston Martin.
Cadillac's senior leadership has moved to **publicly rebut rumours** that Sergio Perez could leave for Williams at season's end.
The remarks come during F1's **summer break**, when driver-market rumours typically peak before the season resumes at Zandvoort.

depth.background: Fernando Alonso, a two-time world champion, has endured a difficult 2026 season at Aston Martin, running near the back of the grid (P21) despite his pedigree — fuelling constant speculation about his future. Separately, Cadillac's debut F1 season brought back veterans Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas, but rumours have circulated that Perez could jump to Williams for 2027 given the new team's growing pains.

stories.title: Ferrari's Leclerc and Hamilton are F1's closest-matched team-mates in qualifying this season
stories.what_happened: Season-long qualifying data shows Leclerc and Hamilton are the most evenly matched team-mate pairing anywhere on the 2026 grid. Leclerc has out-qualified Hamilton in **6 of 11** sessions so far, but his average pace advantage is just **0.050 seconds** — a razor-thin margin over a full lap. Their closest session came in Belgium, where just **0.002 seconds** separated them, while their biggest gap came in Barcelona. The next-tightest team-mate battles on the grid — Cadillac's Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas, and Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and rookie Arvid Lindblad — are both still under a tenth of a second apart, but neither is as close as the Ferrari pairing.
key_points: Of all **11 team-mate pairings** on the 2026 grid, **Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton** have the tightest qualifying battle.
Leclerc leads **6-5** in qualifying sessions won, but is only **0.050 seconds** faster than Hamilton on average.
The closest single gap between them was just **0.002 seconds**, in Belgium.
The next-closest pairings — **Perez/Bottas** at Cadillac and **Lawson/Lindblad** at Racing Bulls — are both still under **0.100 seconds** apart.

depth.background: Comparing team-mates' qualifying times is one of the most trusted ways to judge driver performance in F1, since both drivers use effectively the same car — stripping out most of the machinery differences that make comparing rivals on different teams unreliable. Lewis Hamilton joined Ferrari alongside Charles Leclerc for the 2025 season in one of the sport's most closely watched driver moves in years, pairing a seven-time world champion with the team's long-time leader.

stories.title: Houthi forces launch their biggest ground offensive since 2022, raising fears Yemen could slide back into civil war
stories.what_happened: Since roughly **August 6**, Houthi forces have escalated ground attacks against Saudi-backed Yemeni government positions on multiple fronts, including **Taiz and Marib**, killing at least **30 government troops** in the initial wave. Government forces say they repelled a fresh Houthi assault today on the al-Mafalis front, south of Haifan in Taiz province. This follows Tuesday's separate Houthi strike on the port of Mokha and a Saudi Aramco refinery, which killed 11 people. Analysts describe this as the most substantial Houthi military campaign since the 2022 UN-brokered truce, and warn Yemen risks sliding back into full civil war after years of frozen conflict. Saudi Arabia has so far held back from committing its own troops, but has responded diplomatically: it announced a 13-country Red Sea maritime security coalition on July 30 and signed new defense pacts with Pakistan and Turkey on August 7.
key_points: Houthi forces have launched their **biggest offensive since a 2022 truce** paused Yemen's eight-year civil war.
At least **30 government troops** were killed in the opening wave of attacks around **Taiz and Marib**.
Yemeni government forces say they repelled a fresh Houthi attack on the **al-Mafalis front** south of Haifan today.
Cambridge analyst **Elisabeth Kendall** warns a full relapse into civil war is now a 'looming possibility.'
Saudi Arabia hasn't sent troops but has signed new **defense pacts with Pakistan and Turkey** and formed a 13-country Red Sea maritime coalition.

depth.background: Yemen's civil war has run since **2014**, pitting the Iran-backed Houthi movement — which controls the capital Sanaa and much of the north — against an internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government. A **UN-brokered truce in 2022** froze the front lines and mostly held for years, even as the Houthis separately attacked Red Sea shipping over the Gaza war. That fragile calm cracked on August 11 when Houthi forces struck Yemen's port city of Mokha and a Saudi Aramco refinery, killing 11 — the first fatal Red Sea attack in over a year. The ground war has now reignited too.

thread.previously: On August 11 we reported that Iran-backed Houthi rebels killed 11 people in a strike on Yemen's port city of Mokha and hit a Saudi Aramco refinery, reigniting the Red Sea conflict after roughly a year of relative calm.
thread.changed: The fighting has now spread from the coast to the ground: since around August 6, Houthi forces have pushed a multi-front offensive against Saudi-backed Yemeni government troops around Taiz and Marib, killing at least 30 government soldiers in the opening wave. Analysts call it the most serious Houthi campaign since the 2022 truce that paused Yemen's civil war, and warn a full relapse into war is now a real possibility.

stories.title: US senators demand answers after sailors try to jump off the USS Abraham Lincoln during a record-length deployment
stories.what_happened: Sailors and Marines aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have now been at sea for **more than 260 days**, with **over 200 days** since the ship's last port call — believed to be the longest stretch without shore leave for a US carrier in the modern era. Family members and unnamed crew have told reporters that multiple sailors have either attempted to go overboard or been physically restrained before they could. One family described a sailor texting that '**he hopes he doesn't wake up tomorrow**.' The ship was originally meant to return home months ago but was instead extended and redirected toward the Middle East as part of the US military posture around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. Democratic senators Ruben Gallego and Richard Blumenthal are now demanding the Navy grant Congress an oversight visit and provide a full accounting of overboard and self-harm incidents by **August 27**. The Navy has so far declined to confirm exact numbers, and it's unclear when the strike group will finally return to port.
key_points: The **USS Abraham Lincoln** carrier strike group has been at sea for **more than 260 days**, without a single port call in over **200 days** — a modern-day record.
Multiple sailors have reportedly tried to **jump overboard**, with families describing crew texting that they 'hope they don't wake up tomorrow.'
The ship, carrying roughly **5,000 sailors and Marines**, was diverted from a routine Pacific deployment to the Middle East for Iran-related operations.
Democratic senators **Ruben Gallego and Richard Blumenthal** are demanding a congressional oversight visit and Navy answers by **August 27**.
The Navy has not confirmed how many overboard or self-harm incidents have actually occurred.

depth.background: The USS Abraham Lincoln and its strike group left San Diego on **November 21, 2025**, on what was originally billed as a standard Pacific deployment. As tensions over the **Strait of Hormuz** and Iran escalated through 2026, the Navy redirected the carrier to the Middle East instead of bringing it home. US Navy deployments are typically capped around six to seven months precisely because extended time at sea erodes crew welfare — mental health, family strain, and morale all suffer the longer a ship stays out. This deployment has now blown past that norm by months, with no announced return date.

stories.title: A data center operator is exploring a $100 billion IPO — a sign of how big the AI building boom has gotten
stories.what_happened: According to people familiar with the matter, **Vantage Data Centers** has held preliminary discussions in recent weeks about possible exit paths for its private-equity owners, meeting informally with financial advisers about a stock market listing or a sale. An **IPO** could value the company at around **$100 billion** and raise roughly **$10 billion** for the business — a figure that would make it the largest-ever data center IPO. The company is also weighing a sale, including selling a stake to new investors, as an alternative route. Any deal remains at an early, non-binding stage, and could happen as soon as next year if it proceeds. The exploration comes as AI-driven demand for computing power keeps pushing valuations for data-center operators sharply higher.
key_points: **Vantage Data Centers** is exploring an IPO that could value it at roughly **$100 billion**, which would make it the largest data-center listing ever
The company, backed by private equity firm **Silver Lake** and infrastructure investor **DigitalBridge**, could raise around **$10 billion** in the offering
A **sale**, including a partial stake sale, is also being considered as an alternative to going public
Talks are still preliminary — no formal process has launched, and timing, size, and structure could all change
Vantage has already raised roughly **$11 billion** since late 2023 to build out data centers, underscoring how much capital the AI infrastructure race is consuming

depth.background: **Data centers** are the physical warehouses full of servers and specialized chips (like Nvidia's GPUs) that actually run AI models — every ChatGPT-style answer or AI image is computed inside one. As AI demand has exploded, so has the need for these facilities, and the private equity and infrastructure firms that own them have been pouring in tens of billions of dollars to build bigger ones, faster. Vantage Data Centers is one of the largest such operators globally, and its owners — Silver Lake and DigitalBridge — have already put in over **$9 billion** in equity since 2023 to fund its expansion.

stories.title: A sanctioned Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker sinking off Oman has spread oil across roughly 800 square kilometers of protected coastline
stories.what_happened: Oman's Environment Authority confirmed this week that oil leaking from the grounded, partly-submerged Caroline Bezengi has now reached the country's mainland beaches, around **Ras Madrakah**, some 200 km north of the islands where the tanker first ran into trouble. The slick has expanded dramatically — from roughly **45 square kilometers** on July 26 to about **800 square kilometers** by August 7, according to satellite tracking cited by the Associated Press — with up to **40 km of coastline** now affected. The tanker was carrying close to **one million barrels** of Russian crude when the explosion happened in June, and monsoon-season winds and currents have been pushing the spill further and faster than initially expected.
key_points: The **Caroline Bezengi**, a sanctioned tanker in Russia's "shadow fleet," is sinking after an unexplained explosion in **June**.
It was carrying almost **1 million barrels** of Russian crude bound for Asia when it first reported trouble.
The slick has grown from about **45 sq km** in late July to roughly **800 sq km** by early August, and has now reached Oman's mainland coast.
It threatens the **Hallaniyat Islands** nature reserve, home to nesting sea turtles and the rare **Arabian Sea humpback whale**.
No country or group has claimed responsibility for the **explosion** that crippled the ship, and no party has yet accepted cleanup liability.

depth.background: Since Western sanctions hit Russian oil exports over the Ukraine war, a "shadow fleet" of aging, opaquely-owned tankers has grown up to keep that oil moving — dodging mainstream insurers and price-cap rules by operating outside normal maritime oversight. The **Caroline Bezengi**, a 274-metre tanker identified as part of that fleet, first reported an explosion onboard on **June 8** off Yemen and has been slowly sinking ever since near **Al Qibliyah Island** in Oman's **Hallaniyat Islands** — a protected marine reserve. Because shadow-fleet ships are deliberately hard to trace to a responsible owner or insurer, incidents like this one are difficult to hold anyone accountable for.

stories.title: Leclerc and Gasly wipe their FIA penalty points clean heading into Zandvoort
stories.what_happened: Charles Leclerc entered the resumption of the season with a **clean super licence** after a penalty point from the **2025 Hungarian Grand Prix** — issued for erratic driving while defending his position from George Russell — passed its 12-month expiry. Pierre Gasly's **two penalty points**, handed down for causing a collision with Carlos Sainz at the same race, had already expired on **August 3**. Neither driver currently carries any points on the FIA's rolling ledger, removing any risk of an automatic ban heading into the run-in.
key_points: **Charles Leclerc's** penalty point from the 2025 Hungarian Grand Prix has expired, taking him back to **zero points** on his super licence.
**Pierre Gasly's** two penalty points from a collision with Carlos Sainz at the same race expired on **August 3**.
Under F1 rules, a driver hits **12 penalty points within 12 months** and gets an automatic **one-race ban**.
Leclerc's point had been given for driving erratically while defending against George Russell.
Both drivers head into the resumed season at **Zandvoort** with a clean licence.

depth.background: The FIA's penalty-point system tracks driving infractions on a rolling 12-month basis: points are added for offenses like causing a collision or driving unsafely, and a driver who accumulates 12 or more within that window is automatically banned for one race. Points expire exactly a year after they're issued, so as races from summer 2025 roll off the 12-month window, several drivers are quietly clearing their slate heading into the second half of the 2026 season.

stories.title: Rain threatens to soak every session of F1's final-ever Dutch Grand Prix
stories.what_happened: New weather forecasts for the Dutch Grand Prix weekend, running **August 21-23** at Zandvoort, show a particularly high chance of rain across all three days of track action — practice, the Saturday sprint race, and Sunday's main Grand Prix. It's the first round back after F1's summer break, and it's being promoted as the **last-ever Dutch Grand Prix** at this point in the calendar, which raises the stakes for what could already be a chaotic, rain-affected send-off. Zandvoort's signature steeply banked corners, like the 18-degree 'Hugenholtz' hairpin, become significantly more challenging and prone to accidents when wet. Weekend tickets are already sold out, meaning a rain-soaked weekend would play out in front of a full house.
key_points: Weather forecasts show a **high chance of rain across all three days**, including the sprint race, at Zandvoort.
This is set to be the **last-ever Dutch Grand Prix** at the current calendar slot, adding extra stakes to the weekend.
The 2026 Dutch GP runs **August 21-23**, F1's first race back after the summer break.
Zandvoort's banked corners, including the steep **Turn 3 'Hugenholtz'**, get significantly trickier to drive in the wet.
Weekend tickets for the race are already **sold out**, so a washout would disappoint a packed crowd.

depth.background: The Dutch Grand Prix returned to F1's calendar in 2021 after a 35-year absence, driven largely by the popularity of home favorite Max Verstappen, and quickly became one of the most electric atmospheres on the calendar thanks to its passionate orange-clad crowds at the seaside Zandvoort circuit. The track is known for its unusually steep, banked corners — a layout borrowed from oval racing — which makes it especially demanding when conditions are wet and grip is reduced. This edition is being billed as the **final running of the race**, adding sentimental weight on top of the usual championship stakes.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake death toll rises to 273 as rescuers enter a 'final phase' — but the missing count drops sharply as thousands are found
stories.what_happened: Colombia's disaster-management agency says the confirmed death toll has climbed to **273**, with 3,824 injured, as of the latest count. Crucially, the number of people still classified as missing has fallen dramatically — from more than 2,700 reported missing earlier in the week to **377** now — as search teams worked through the rubble and located thousands of previously unaccounted-for residents. One notable rescue: a 32-year-old woman was pulled out alive in Pereira after more than 36 hours trapped. Authorities say rescue operations have now entered their 'final phase', with international help including roughly 40 US search-and-rescue personnel. The quake damaged over 200 roads, five airports, and 44 water systems (aqueducts) across the affected region.
key_points: The death toll from Colombia's **7.4-magnitude earthquake** has risen to **273**, with **3,824** people reported injured.
The number still listed as missing has fallen sharply to **377**, down from over 2,700 reported missing days earlier, as many were located.
A **32-year-old woman was pulled alive** from rubble in Pereira after being trapped for more than **36 hours**.
Rescue operations have entered a **'final phase'**, with US urban search-and-rescue teams (~40 people) helping local first responders.
More than **200 roads**, 5 airports, and 44 aqueducts were damaged, hitting the hard-hit Pereira and Cali regions.

depth.background: A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia on **August 10**, centered near San José del Palmar in Chocó department — the country's strongest quake in a century. It flattened buildings and infrastructure across the Pereira and Cali regions, triggering a mass rescue operation. Colombia's new government faced criticism over aid access and the pace of the response in the disaster's first days.

thread.previously: We reported the death toll had passed 265 with over 2,700 people still reported missing, as rescue teams struggled to reach the earthquake's epicenter.
thread.changed: The death toll has risen only modestly to 273, but the missing count has collapsed to 377 as thousands were located — and officials now say rescue operations are entering their 'final phase'.

stories.title: Australia win the toss and bat first as the historic Bangladesh Test begins in Darwin
stories.what_happened: Australia won the toss and captain **Pat Cummins** elected to bat first on a green Darwin surface in humid conditions, with opener **Travis Head** expecting a tough opening period against the new ball. Australia's confirmed XI is: Jake Weatherald, Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins (captain), Nathan Lyon, and Josh Hazlewood. Both Green and Webster won selection battles for their all-rounder spots, and Lyon returns to the side after sitting out the back end of the Ashes with a hamstring injury. This marks the first time in over a year that Australia's leading pace trio — Cummins, Hazlewood, and Starc — has played together. Bangladesh has named Ebadot Hossain and Mahmudul Hasan in its own XI as the tourists begin their first Test series on Australian soil in 23 years.

The confirmed Australia XI includes **Cameron Green and Beau Webster**, both winning selection battles for the spot.
**Nathan Lyon returns** after missing the back end of the Ashes with a hamstring injury.

This is Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**, marking a historic return fixture.

depth.background: Bangladesh last toured Australia for a Test series back in 2003, when Australia won comfortably — so this five-day match at Darwin's Marrara Cricket Ground, starting the current series, is being treated as a genuinely historic fixture for Bangladeshi cricket. Australia has been juggling injuries and form questions in its bowling attack over the past year, including during the recent Ashes series, which is why the reunion of its three most experienced fast bowlers together is being watched closely.

depth.background: Bangladesh have toured Australia for Test cricket only rarely, and not at all in over two decades — a gap driven by scheduling, cricket-calendar priorities, and Australia's traditionally packed home summer. Darwin, in Australia's tropical Northern Territory, is an unusual and rarely-used Test venue, chosen partly to give Bangladesh conditions (heat, humidity) closer to what they're used to at home, even though the pitch and bounce still differ sharply from subcontinental cricket. stories.title: Bangladesh still hasn't decided if its PM will visit India for the BRICS summit
stories.what_happened: Bangladesh's Foreign Minister **Khalilur Rahman** said the government is still **'currently reviewing'** Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's invitation for PM Tarique Rahman to attend the **18th BRICS Summit**, scheduled for **September 12-13 in New Delhi**. India confirmed on August 4 that it had extended the invite, with Rahman invited in his capacity as **BIMSTEC chairperson** rather than strictly as Bangladesh's head of government — a distinction Dhaka is weighing carefully. The foreign minister noted Rahman has multiple overseas commitments to juggle, including a planned trip to the **UN General Assembly** in New York, and that all engagements need to be considered together before a decision is made. This follows an earlier, still-unconfirmed invitation from Modi in February for a full bilateral visit with Rahman's family.
key_points: India confirmed on **August 4** it had invited Bangladesh PM **Tarique Rahman** to the **18th BRICS Summit** in New Delhi.
Bangladesh Foreign Minister **Khalilur Rahman** says the government is **'currently reviewing'** the invitation, with no decision yet.
The summit is scheduled for **September 12-13** in New Delhi; Rahman also has a UN General Assembly trip to weigh alongside it.
The invite came as **BIMSTEC chairperson**, not specifically as Bangladesh's PM — a nuance being parsed closely in Dhaka.
This is Modi's **second invitation** to Rahman this year, after a February invite for a bilateral visit went unanswered with a firm date.

depth.background: India-Bangladesh relations have been unsettled since **Sheikh Hasina's** government fell and she went into exile, with **Tarique Rahman** (leader of the BNP) now heading Bangladesh's government. Rahman notably chose Malaysia and China, not India, for his first official overseas trip after taking office — a signal read in Delhi as a deliberate distancing. Tensions were compounded further after Hasina gave a speech from Delhi that unsettled the relationship. **BRICS** is a bloc of major emerging economies (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, and now expanded membership) that holds an annual summit; India is hosting this year's edition. Modi has now extended two separate invitations to Rahman in 2026 — one for a bilateral visit in February, and a follow-up for the BRICS summit — as India tries to keep a diplomatic door open despite the frosty start.

stories.title: Parliament curbs states' power to tax mining companies, in a win for the Centre over resource-rich states
stories.what_happened: The **Lok Sabha** passed the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 on **August 12**, and the **Rajya Sabha** cleared it the following day, **August 13**. The bill inserts a new **Section 9D**, under which states cannot impose taxes, cess, or other levies on mineral rights or mineral-bearing land based on the quantity or value of the mineral, or the royalty payable, except within conditions the Centre prescribes. The Centre will directly regulate major minerals — coal, limestone, iron ore, copper and manganese among them — while states retain authority over 49 minor minerals. The law also invalidates any state levies from before this amendment that companies haven't yet paid or that states haven't yet recovered, though money already collected will not have to be refunded. The bill becomes law once it receives the President's assent.
key_points: Parliament passed the **Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026**.
It bars states from taxing **mineral rights or mineral-bearing land** except on terms the Centre allows.
The Centre keeps control of major minerals like **coal, iron ore, copper and manganese**; states keep 49 minor minerals.
The law also **wipes out un-recovered past state levies**, though taxes already collected won't be refunded.
Mines Minister **G Kishan Reddy** says the goal is a **uniform mineral tax rate** nationwide, not less state revenue.

depth.background: This fight goes back to a landmark 2024 Supreme Court ruling that affirmed states' constitutional power to levy their own taxes on mineral rights and mineral-bearing land — on top of the royalty they already collect — and even allowed them to claim it retrospectively. Mineral-rich states like Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal moved to send large back-dated tax demands to mining companies, including state-run giants like Coal India, following that ruling. The Centre has now used ordinary legislation to substantially narrow what that Supreme Court ruling opened up.

stories.title: A Pakistan-linked militant front threatens Kashmiri Pandit government employees days before India's Independence Day
stories.what_happened: An outfit calling itself the United Liberation Council, which security officials say is a front for Lashkar-e-Taiba, posted an online letter listing the names and phone numbers of Kashmiri Pandit employees working under the Prime Minister's Special Employment Package. In response, the Jammu and Kashmir administration told roughly **2,800 employees** — Pandits, other migrants and those on the rehabilitation package — to stay away from their physical offices and work from home until **August 20**. Many of the named employees and their families have since left the Valley for Jammu, saying they intend to return only once the Independence Day period passes. Police have responded by stepping up night patrols, checkpoints and surveillance, including drones, at vulnerable locations and key entry and exit points across the region.
key_points: The **United Liberation Council**, a front for the Pakistan-based group Lashkar-e-Taiba, circulated an online letter naming Kashmiri Pandit employees along with their phone numbers
Around **2,800 Pandit, migrant and rehabilitation-package employees** have been told to work from home until **August 20**
Many affected families have fled to Jammu, planning to return only after the **August 15** celebrations
Police have added night patrols, checkpoints, frisking and drone surveillance across Srinagar and south Kashmir
The threat lands just before India's **80th Independence Day**, when security in the Valley is already at its tightest

depth.background: Kashmiri Pandits are Hindus native to the Kashmir Valley who were driven out by militant violence in a mass exodus in **1989-90**, during the early years of an insurgency against Indian rule. In recent years the government has run a rehabilitation package offering government jobs to encourage some Pandit families to return, part of a broader push to show that normal life has returned to Jammu and Kashmir since Delhi revoked the region's special autonomous status in **2019**. Lashkar-e-Taiba, the group blamed for the 2008 Mumbai attacks, has repeatedly targeted this return-and-resettlement push as a symbol of India's presence in the Valley it wants to disrupt.

stories.title: Jasprit Bumrah ruled out of the Sri Lanka Tests as India hands uncapped Auqib Nabi a shock call-up
stories.what_happened: The BCCI announced a 15-member squad for the two-match Test series against Sri Lanka, naming Shubman Gill as captain and KL Rahul as vice-captain. Bumrah was left out entirely as he continues recovering from the knee injury sustained during India's ODI series in England, and uncapped fast bowler Auqib Nabi — who took 104 wickets in his last two Ranji Trophy seasons for Jammu and Kashmir, including 60 in this year's title-winning campaign — was named as his replacement. Gill, who had been under an injury cloud after hurting his finger in the warm-up match against a Sri Lanka Cricket XI, has since been passed fit to lead. Sai Sudharsan was separately ruled out of the series with a fractured toe. The first of the two Tests begins August 15 at Galle.
key_points: **Jasprit Bumrah** misses the two-match series as he continues recovering from a left-knee injury picked up in the England ODIs
**Shubman Gill** has been declared fit to captain the side after a finger scare in the warm-up match
**Auqib Nabi**, 26, earns his maiden India call-up after taking **104 wickets** across his last two Ranji Trophy seasons
KL Rahul is vice-captain; **Sai Sudharsan** is also out of the series with a fractured toe
The first Test starts **August 15** in Galle — India's first red-ball tour of Sri Lanka in **nine years**

depth.background: India last toured Sri Lanka for a Test series in 2017, when Virat Kohli's side completed a 3-0 clean sweep. This series is part of the 2025-27 World Test Championship (WTC) cycle, in which India currently sit fifth in the standings and Sri Lanka sixth. Bumrah, India's premier fast bowler, has been carefully managed through injuries in recent months, while allrounder Ravindra Jadeja's fitness has also been closely watched heading into this tour.
