stories.title: FSSAI warns food influencers as data shows 98% of their ads now break advertising rules
stories.what_happened: FSSAI issued a public advisory this week cautioning food influencers and celebrities to carefully vet any brand claims before endorsing them, warning that promoting **unverified or misleading food claims** can lead to legal consequences for the endorser, not just the brand. The advisory came alongside fresh data from ASCI showing the ad-violation rate for influencer content has climbed sharply: **93% of ads were flagged as non-compliant or needing modification in 2021-22**, rising to **98% in 2025-26**. Over the same period, ASCI processed **37,532 total ad-violation cases**, of which **21.12% involved influencers**. FSSAI specifically called out common claims like 'boosts immunity' or 'rich in nutrients' as red flags when a brand can't substantiate them under existing food-safety and advertising rules. The advisory asks influencers to verify claims are truthful and compliant before lending their name and reach to a brand.
key_points: India's food regulator **FSSAI** warned influencers and celebrities against making unverified health or nutrition claims for food products.
The share of influencer food/health ads found non-compliant with rules jumped from **93% in 2021-22 to 98% in 2025-26**, per ASCI data.
**ASCI processed 37,532 ad-violation cases** in the period; over a fifth (**21.12%**) involved influencers specifically.
FSSAI singled out vague claims like 'boosts immunity' or 'rich in nutrients' when brands can't back them up with evidence.
Influencers who promote unverified claims can now face **legal consequences**, not just a warning.

depth.background: India's influencer-marketing industry has exploded over the past few years, and food and health brands are among the heaviest users of influencer endorsements to sell everything from supplements to snacks. The **Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI)**, a self-regulatory body, has been tracking ad-compliance rates for years, and **FSSAI** (the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India) is the government regulator responsible for enforcing food-safety and labeling law. Regulators in India have increasingly focused on influencers specifically because their endorsements are seen as more trusted — and thus more persuasive, and more risky when false — than traditional ads.

stories.title: Delhi's H1N1 swine flu cases jump nearly sixfold this monsoon, with hospitals seeing a steady stream of patients
stories.what_happened: Delhi has logged **1,349 confirmed H1N1 cases** in 2026 so far, compared with just 229 over the same stretch last year — a nearly sixfold jump. Hospitals across the city, including major private facilities, report a steady stream of patients presenting with cough, cold, and high fever, with some outpatient departments seeing 7 to 10 H1N1 cases a day. Delhi's Health Minister Pankaj Singh said the government has ramped up testing across the city and set up dedicated wards and rooms in government hospitals to handle the rise. Doctors at AIIMS Delhi and elsewhere attribute the spike to the usual monsoon pattern of shifting temperatures, which favours the spread of influenza viruses.
key_points: Delhi has recorded **1,349 H1N1 cases** so far this year, versus just **229** in the same period of 2025 — almost a **sixfold rise**.
Hospitals report seeing around **7–10 H1N1 patients daily** in outpatient departments during the surge.
Delhi's Health Minister Pankaj Singh says **regular testing** is underway citywide and dedicated wards have been set up.
Doctors say **monsoon-season temperature swings** are a key driver of the seasonal rise in influenza cases.
The surge follows a broader pattern of **rising flu activity** across north India during the monsoon.

depth.background: H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, is a strain of seasonal influenza that tends to spike in India during the monsoon months as temperature and humidity swings help the virus spread more easily. Delhi's health system regularly tracks these seasonal infection numbers and adjusts hospital capacity accordingly.

stories.title: India's Monsoon Session of Parliament ends today, passing 11 bills after weeks of NEET-protest disruption
stories.what_happened: Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairman C P Radhakrishnan adjourned their respective Houses **sine die** on Thursday, officially closing the Monsoon Session. Despite the disruptions, both Houses together passed **11 bills** during the session, with the **Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill** clearing the Rajya Sabha by voice vote in the closing sitting. The Lok Sabha's final day opened with six stanzas of **Vande Mataram**, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi both present in the chamber. The Opposition's core demand — that Amit Shah personally address the Jantar Mantar police-crackdown allegations — was never formally resolved on the floor before the session closed.
key_points: Parliament's **Monsoon Session** was adjourned **sine die** today, closing on its originally scheduled date.
**11 bills** were passed across both Houses over the course of the session.
The **Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill** cleared the Rajya Sabha by **voice vote** in the final sitting.
The session opened on **July 20** and was repeatedly disrupted by protests over the **NEET-UG paper leak** police crackdown.
The final Lok Sabha sitting opened with **Vande Mataram**, with PM Modi and Congress's Rahul Gandhi both present.

depth.background: "Sine die" adjournment means a legislative session ends completely with no date set to resume — different from a normal recess. This Monsoon Session began on **July 20** already under pressure, as the Opposition demanded Home Minister Amit Shah personally explain the police response to a **NEET-UG paper-leak protest** at Jantar Mantar that Delhi Police say injured roughly **60 protesters and 118 police personnel**. That standoff, alongside disputes like the contested **FCRA** bill (which lets government seize NGOs' foreign-funded assets and was instead referred to a joint parliamentary panel), repeatedly disrupted proceedings through the session.

thread.previously: We reported the Opposition was blocking normal business, demanding Home Minister Amit Shah personally address the police response to the July 20 NEET-protest clash at Jantar Mantar, and that the standoff was eating into the Monsoon Session's last sitting days before its scheduled August 13 close.
thread.changed: The session has now ended on schedule — Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairman C P Radhakrishnan adjourned both Houses sine die today, with 11 bills passed, including the Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill by voice vote, despite disruptions continuing through the final days.

stories.title: Tata Trusts formally kicks off the search for Chandrasekaran's successor, with Tata Steel's T V Narendran an early frontrunner
stories.what_happened: The Sir Dorabji Tata Trust's trustees passed a resolution to set up a **Selection Committee** "as soon as possible" to recommend a new Tata Sons chairman, as required under the company's Articles of Association. The committee will have **five members**: three jointly nominated by the two Tata Trusts, one from the Tata Sons board, and one independent outside member chosen by the board — with the two trusts also picking the committee's chair from among their three nominees. Early reporting names **T V Narendran**, Tata Steel's Global CEO and MD since 1988 with the group, as a leading contender, alongside Tata Sons CFO **Saurabh Agrawal** and Tata Motors MD/CEO **Shailesh Chandra**. Noel Tata, who chairs Tata Trusts, can only step in as an *interim* Tata Sons chairman in exigent circumstances — not take the role permanently — under the same 2022 rules that created this succession puzzle in the first place.
key_points: Tata Trusts passed a resolution to set up a **five-member Selection Committee** to recommend the next Tata Sons chairman.
**T V Narendran**, Tata Steel's global CEO and a 38-year Tata veteran, has emerged as an early frontrunner.
Other reported contenders include Tata Sons CFO **Saurabh Agrawal** and Tata Motors chief **Shailesh Chandra**.
**Noel Tata** could only step in as *interim* chairman in an emergency — he can't hold the job permanently while also chairing Tata Trusts.
The process formally begins just **days before** the group's **August 18** AGM, with no chairman yet named.

depth.background: Tata Sons, the holding company for the roughly **$165 billion** Tata Group, is majority-owned by two philanthropic bodies — the **Sir Dorabji Tata Trust** and **Sir Ratan Tata Trust** — which together control who becomes chairman. N. Chandrasekaran has led Tata Sons since **2017** and told the trusts on **August 12** that he will not seek reappointment when his term ends in **February 2027**. Under 2022 governance rules, the Tata Trusts chairman (currently Noel Tata) cannot simultaneously hold the Tata Sons chairmanship, which rules out the family's most obvious internal candidate from taking the job outright.

thread.previously: We reported that after Chandrasekaran said he wouldn't seek reappointment, Tata Sons had to run its succession process for the first time since 2017 — and that the natural internal candidate, Noel Tata, already chairs Tata Trusts, which the group's 2022 rules block from also holding the Tata Sons chairmanship.
thread.changed: Tata Trusts has now formally passed a resolution to set up a five-member Selection Committee to recommend Chandrasekaran's successor, and Tata Steel CEO T V Narendran has emerged as an early frontrunner alongside Tata Sons CFO Saurabh Agrawal and Tata Motors chief Shailesh Chandra.

stories.title: Scotland thump Canada by 170 runs in Dundee rematch to boost their 2027 World Cup qualification hopes
stories.what_happened: Scotland posted a commanding **347 for 7** batting first at Forthill in Dundee, then bowled out Canada for just **177**, winning by **170 runs**. Left-arm bowler Lyle Robertson was the standout performer, taking **6 wickets for 52 runs** to earn Player of the Match honours. The comprehensive win comes just a week after the two sides met in a far closer contest, which Scotland won by only 9 runs (281/7 to Canada's 272), underlining how much more dominant this second meeting was.
key_points: Scotland beat Canada by **170 runs** in Dundee, posting **347/7** before bowling Canada out for just **177**.
Left-armer **Lyle Robertson** starred with **6 wickets for 52 runs**, earning Player of the Match.
The result comes just days after Scotland edged the same opponent by a much tighter **9 runs** in an earlier meeting.
The match was part of the **ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2**, a qualification pathway toward the 2027 World Cup.

The two sides had already met earlier this month in a tight 9-run Scotland win, making this rematch a chance for Scotland to build a bigger points cushion.

stories.title: Ferrari plans a bigger engine upgrade at Monza — double its last power gain — as it chases Mercedes for the F1 title
stories.what_happened: Reports from multiple F1 outlets say Ferrari is preparing to bring an engine upgrade worth roughly **15 extra horsepower** to the Italian Grand Prix at Monza in early September — Ferrari's home race. That would be about double the ~7hp gain the team's engine update delivered at the Austrian Grand Prix in July, its first use of a development token this season. Ferrari says it has stuck to a 'little and often' approach to upgrades on its SF-26 car rather than saving its budget for one large step, and insists it hasn't breached F1's cost cap doing so. The team returns from F1's summer break at the Dutch Grand Prix in Zandvoort before the Monza upgrade arrives.
key_points: Ferrari is set to bring roughly a **15-horsepower** engine upgrade to September's Italian Grand Prix at Monza
That's about **double** the ~7hp gain its engine update delivered at the Austrian Grand Prix earlier this season
The upgrade uses one of Ferrari's limited allowance of in-season engine development tokens under F1's 2026 rules
Mercedes has won the first six races of the year and leads the constructors' championship by **72 points**
Ferrari is running a **'little and often'** upgrade strategy rather than saving everything for one big step

depth.background: F1's 2026 technical rules brought in all-new power units with a bigger role for electric power, and to keep costs in check, manufacturers get only a small number of allowed in-season upgrade opportunities rather than unlimited development. Mercedes built an early advantage this season, winning the first six races, with rookie **Kimi Antonelli** leading the drivers' championship. Ferrari, chasing that gap with **Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc**, used its first upgrade token at the Austrian Grand Prix in July for a modest power gain and has been developing its car incrementally since.

stories.title: A US judge dismisses the criminal case against Gautam Adani — and Adani calls it 'humility, not vindication'
stories.what_happened: Judge Nicholas G. Garaufis of the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York ruled on **Aug. 11** to dismiss, with prejudice, three criminal charges against Gautam Adani, his nephew Sagar Adani, and Adani Green Energy CEO Vneet Jaain — conspiracy to commit securities fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and securities fraud. The judge granted the dismissal at the DOJ's own request, but criticized the department for "irregularities," including bypassing its own investigators and what he described as colluding with defense counsel, and he refused to dismiss two related charges against **five other, non-Adani defendants** in the same case, saying prosecutors hadn't adequately justified that request. Court filings and the judge's own questioning probed whether Adani's November 2024 pledge to invest **$10 billion** in the United States played a role in the DOJ's decision to drop the case; a lawyer for Adani confirmed in a July filing that the group was "amenable" to following through on that pledge as part of resolving matters. Adani broke his silence on **Aug. 12** in a public address, saying the dismissal left him with "humility rather than a sense of vindication," and stating, "Trust is greater than any legal right." He drew a parallel to 2023, when — after the Hindenburg report triggered a stock rout — Adani Group was legally entitled to proceed with a ₹20,000 crore share sale but chose to cancel it and return investors' money instead.
key_points: Judge Nicholas Garaufis dismissed **three fraud and bribery charges** against Gautam Adani, his nephew Sagar Adani, and a top Adani Green executive, **with prejudice**.
The original indictment alleged a **$265 million bribery scheme** tied to solar power contracts in India.
The judge **sharply criticized** the DOJ for 'irregularities,' including bypassing its own investigators, even while granting the dismissal.
He specifically questioned whether Adani's pledge to invest **$10 billion in the US** influenced the DOJ's decision to drop the case.
Adani responded not with celebration but with a public statement: **'Trust is greater than any legal right.'**

depth.background: Gautam Adani is Asia's second-richest man and chairs the **Adani Group**, the Indian conglomerate that runs ports, power plants, airports, cement, and green-energy projects across the country. In November 2024, US prosecutors under the Biden administration indicted Adani and several executives, accusing them of paying over $250 million in bribes to Indian officials to win solar-power supply contracts, and of concealing this from US investors while raising capital there — allegations Adani has always denied. The case had shadowed Adani Group's stock price and its access to US capital markets for nearly two years, on top of a separate 2023 short-seller report by Hindenburg Research that briefly wiped tens of billions off the group's market value.

stories.title: The Hundred's Eliminator picture is set: Sunrisers Leeds through after Birmingham Phoenix knock out MI London
stories.what_happened: Birmingham Phoenix beat MI London in their final group match, a result that eliminated MI London from contention and confirmed Sunrisers Leeds as the fourth and final qualifier for the knockout stage. That completes the picture for the men's competition: Manchester Super Giants will play Sunrisers Leeds in the Eliminator at The Oval on August 14, with the winner advancing to face Trent Rockets — who topped the table and already have a direct spot — in the final at Lord's on August 16.
key_points: **Birmingham Phoenix** beat **MI London** in the last regular-season match, eliminating them and sending **Sunrisers Leeds** through instead.
The men's **Eliminator** is now confirmed: **Manchester Super Giants vs Sunrisers Leeds**, August 14 at The Oval.
**Trent Rockets** already secured top spot and a direct place in the final at Lord's on August 16.
The Eliminator winner will face Trent Rockets in the final.
The result closes out group-stage play across the men's competition.

depth.background: The Hundred is England's 100-ball franchise cricket competition, with eight men's and eight women's teams. Going into the last day of group games, Trent Rockets had already locked up first place and a direct final berth, while Manchester Super Giants had secured the other guaranteed spot — the Eliminator. The final qualification slot, between MI London and Sunrisers Leeds, came down to the last matches of the group stage.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake toll climbs past 265 as more than 2,700 remain reported missing
stories.what_happened: As of Wednesday, Colombian authorities had confirmed at least **265 dead**, a sharp rise from the 220-227 figures reported the previous day, with officials warning the number will likely keep climbing as rescuers reach areas still cut off by blocked roads. Separately, volunteer-run tracking databases — which count family reports the government hasn't yet verified — put the number of people still unaccounted for at **more than 2,700**. Rescue crews have logged over **70 aftershocks** since the initial quake and are using thermal-imaging drones, cadaver dogs and specialized rubble-clearing equipment to keep searching in Cali, where a woman was pulled alive from debris almost 30 hours after the quake and a baby was rescued from a collapsed apartment building. The material toll is also severe: more than **1,100 homes destroyed** and **8,300 more damaged** across the affected region. Colombia had initially asked for help from only the US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel, but has since widened its request, with Peru now confirming it will send volunteer rescuers too.
key_points: The confirmed death toll from Monday's **7.4-magnitude earthquake** has climbed past **265**, up from the 220-227 range reported a day earlier.
Volunteer networks tracking family reports say more than **2,700 people are still unaccounted for**, far above the government's own missing-persons count.
Rescue teams have recorded more than **70 aftershocks** and are using **thermal-imaging drones and cadaver dogs** to search collapsed buildings in Cali.
More than **1,100 homes have been destroyed** and **8,300 damaged**, with roads into the epicenter near San José del Palmar still blocked.
Dramatic rescues continue even past the 72-hour survival window — including a **baby pulled alive from a collapsed Cali apartment block**.

depth.background: A **7.4-magnitude earthquake** struck Colombia's Pacific coast on Monday, the strongest the country has recorded in a decade. It hit hardest in the western Chocó region, near the town of San José del Palmar, and shook the capital Bogotá and the city of Cali. The disaster is the **first major crisis test** for Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, whose government initially limited international rescue offers to just four countries — a decision now under public criticism as the scale of the damage has become clearer.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported the confirmed death toll had passed 220-227, the critical 72-hour survival window had effectively closed, and Colombia's government was facing backlash for initially limiting foreign rescue offers to just four countries.
thread.changed: The confirmed toll has now climbed past 265, volunteer networks report more than 2,700 people still unaccounted for, and rescuers using thermal drones and dog teams have kept pulling survivors — including a baby — from the rubble in Cali even after the survival window closed.

stories.title: Supreme Court signals it will send the Krishna Janmabhoomi-Shahi Idgah 'who represents Hindus' dispute back to the Allahabad High Court
stories.what_happened: The Supreme Court was hearing an appeal from plaintiffs in the original 2020 suit (suit no. 1, which seeks removal of the mosque), who challenged an **Allahabad High Court ruling** that let a different, later group of petitioners (suit no. 17) be treated as the representative voice for 'all devotees of Lord Krishna' in the case. The bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva observed that the High Court had made this designation **without issuing notice to the plaintiffs in the other suits**, meaning those parties never got a chance to argue against it. The judges indicated they are inclined to send the representation question back down to the Allahabad High Court so it can be reheard properly, with all plaintiffs given notice and an opportunity to be heard this time. The Court granted an adjournment until **September 2**, when it is expected to formalise this order.
key_points: The Supreme Court said it is **inclined to remand** a key procedural fight in the long-running Krishna Janmabhoomi-Shahi Idgah case back to the **Allahabad High Court**.
The dispute is over **which plaintiffs get to represent** 'all devotees of Lord Krishna' in the underlying suit — not the core temple-mosque dispute itself.
The High Court had let one Hindu party (suit no. 17) represent all devotees **without formally notifying** the plaintiffs from other, earlier suits, including suit no. 1.
A bench of **Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva** wants all plaintiffs given a fair hearing on the representation question before the case moves forward.
The matter has been adjourned to **September 2** for a formal order.

depth.background: The Krishna Janmabhoomi-Shahi Idgah dispute is one of India's most sensitive ongoing religious-property cases, centred on a mosque in Mathura that Hindu petitioners say sits on the site of Lord Krishna's birthplace, and which some groups want removed or partially reclaimed. It sits alongside the Ayodhya Ram Mandir dispute as one of a handful of major Hindu-Muslim religious site disputes working through India's courts over the past decade, and both sides have long anticipated it could become similarly high-profile. Multiple separate lawsuits by different Hindu petitioner groups have been filed over the years, each claiming to represent devotees' interests — which is what created today's narrower procedural fight over who actually gets to be the 'lead' plaintiff group in court.

stories.title: Spain just had its first total solar eclipse since 1905 — and it's only the opener in an unheard-of three-eclipse run through 2028
stories.what_happened: On Wednesday, the Moon's shadow swept from **Greenland and Iceland across northern Spain** as the Sun set, delivering totality — the brief window when the Moon fully blocks the Sun — to an estimated **15 million people**, most of them in Spain. It was the **first total solar eclipse over mainland Europe since 1999** and mainland Spain's first since **1905**. Scientists used the rare darkness to study the Sun's **corona**, the outer atmosphere normally invisible in daylight, which affects space weather that can disrupt satellites and power grids. What makes this moment bigger than a single afternoon is the calendar that follows: Spain will see a second total eclipse on **August 2, 2027**, then an annular eclipse on **January 26, 2028** — a three-eclipse sequence astronomers are calling the 'Iberian trio', the first cluster of total eclipses over mainland Europe this century.
key_points: Monday's eclipse was Spain's first total solar eclipse in mainland territory since **1905** — 121 years.
A second total eclipse will cross Spain again on **August 2, 2027**, visible from the Iberian Peninsula down into North Africa and the Middle East.
A third eclipse — an **annular** ('ring of fire') eclipse where the Moon doesn't fully cover the Sun — follows on **January 26, 2028**.
Astronomers are calling it the **'Iberian trio'**, an occurrence so rare that few countries have experienced three eclipses this close together.
The totality path this week reached as far as **Palma, Valencia, Zaragoza, Bilbao and León**, with observers getting up to 1 minute 50 seconds of darkness.

depth.background: Total solar eclipses happen somewhere on Earth every year or two, but any single spot on the planet typically waits **centuries** between them, because the Moon's shadow is only about 100 miles wide and sweeps across a thin, fast-moving path. Mainland Spain's last one was in **1905**; mainland Europe as a whole hadn't seen one since **1999**. That's what made this week's event, and the discovery that two more are coming within two years, so unusual to scientists who track these cycles.

thread.previously: We covered Tuesday's eclipse as it happened: totality began around 15:34 GMT and swept from Iceland to Spain, lasting up to 2 minutes 18 seconds, watched by an estimated 15 million people, and coinciding with the Perseid meteor shower.
thread.changed: Now that the event has passed, the bigger story is emerging: this wasn't a one-off. It's the first of **three consecutive total or annular solar eclipses to cross Spain by 2028** — a concentration of eclipses astronomers say almost no country has ever seen in such a short span, turning Spain into a hub for eclipse tourism for the rest of the decade.

stories.title: India's retail inflation hits a 19-month high of 4.45% in July, driven by pricier food
stories.what_happened: The National Statistics Office reported that India's retail inflation rose to 4.45% in July, its highest level in 19 months and up from 4.38% in June. The increase was mainly driven by food prices, where inflation rose to 5.52% from 5.32% the month before. This marks the second consecutive month inflation has printed above the RBI's 4% target, following sixteen straight months where it had stayed below that level. The RBI's own projections, released alongside its August rate decision, anticipate inflation will keep climbing in the near term and peak around 5.9% in the October-December quarter of this fiscal year, before easing again.
key_points: **Consumer price index (CPI) inflation** rose to **4.45% in July**, up from 4.38% in June — the **highest reading in 19 months**.
**Food inflation** was the main driver, climbing to **5.52%** from 5.32% the previous month.
This is the **second straight month** that inflation has stayed above the **RBI's 4% target**, after 16 months of running below it.
The RBI itself expects headline inflation to keep rising and **peak near 5.9% in the October-December quarter**.
Data was released by the **National Statistics Office (NSO)** on August 12.

depth.background: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures how much prices for a broad basket of everyday goods and services — like food, fuel and housing — have changed for typical households, and it's India's main gauge of retail inflation. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) targets keeping CPI inflation around 4%, using it as the main input for interest-rate decisions. Just a week earlier, the RBI's rate-setting committee had held its key policy rate steady at 5.25% for a fourth straight meeting, citing a wish for 'greater clarity' on where inflation was heading before acting either way.

stories.title: A total solar eclipse sweeps across mainland Europe for the first time since 1999
stories.what_happened: Totality began around **15:34 GMT** and swept west to east across the path, lasting up to two minutes eighteen seconds at its longest point. An estimated **15 million people**, most of them in Spain, were positioned inside the path of totality, with Iceland catching the eclipse in the late afternoon before the Moon's shadow raced on toward Spain near sunset. The event doubled as a triple sky show: it coincided with the peak of the **Perseid meteor shower** and followed a rare six-planet alignment visible before dawn the same day. Scientists in Spain and Iceland used the brief window of darkness to study the Sun's corona, a layer of the Sun's atmosphere that is normally washed out by direct sunlight and can only be observed properly during totality or with specialized instruments.
key_points: The Moon fully blocked the Sun over **Iceland, Greenland and northern Spain** — the first total eclipse seen from mainland Europe in **27 years**.
Up to **15 million people**, mostly in Spain, sat inside the narrow 'path of totality' where the sky went dark in daytime.
Totality lasted up to **2 minutes 18 seconds** at its longest point along the path.
The eclipse coincided with the peak of the **Perseid meteor shower** and a rare pre-dawn alignment of six planets.
Scientists used the brief darkness to study the Sun's **corona**, its outer atmosphere that's normally invisible in daylight.

depth.background: A total solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between the Earth and the Sun, and its shadow is small enough that only a narrow strip of the planet — the 'path of totality' — experiences full darkness. Because the Moon's shadow is only about 100-160 km wide, most eclipses cross oceans or sparsely populated land; this is the **first one to sweep across mainland Europe since 1999**, and the first ever recorded from the Iberian Peninsula in over a century. The path today ran from Siberian Russia through Greenland and Iceland before reaching northern Spain and Portugal just before sunset.

stories.title: Tata stocks drag Sensex lower as investors digest Chandrasekaran's shock resignation, oil pressure adds to the drop
stories.what_happened: India's benchmark stock indices closed lower on August 12: the **Sensex fell 187.90 points, or 0.24%, to 77,966.35**, while the **Nifty50 fell 35.75 points to 24,435.95** — the second straight day of losses. The decline was led by Tata Group stocks: **TCS fell roughly 4%**, with **Tata Steel down 1.73%** and **Tata Motors down 1.61%**, as investors reacted to chairman N. Chandrasekaran's surprise announcement that he'll step down when his current term ends in February 2027. That succession uncertainty compounded separate pressure from rising **Brent crude oil prices**, which climbed toward $88 a barrel amid the ongoing standoff over the Strait of Hormuz — a key chokepoint for global oil shipments. Not every stock fell: IndusInd Bank, UltraTech Cement, and Power Grid were among the day's gainers.
key_points: **Sensex fell 187.90 points (0.24%)** to close at **77,966.35**; **Nifty50 fell 35.75 points** to 24,435.95.
**Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) dropped around 4%**, the single biggest drag on the index.
**Tata Steel** fell 1.73% and **Tata Motors** fell 1.61%, as Tata group stocks led the market's decline.
The fall comes a day after **Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran announced he'll step down** when his term ends in February 2027.
Rising **crude oil prices**, driven by the ongoing Strait of Hormuz standoff, added separate pressure on the broader market.

depth.background: Tata Consultancy Services is the Tata Group's largest and most valuable listed company, so it carries outsized weight in India's benchmark indices — when TCS moves sharply, it can single-handedly pull the whole market. This comes right after N. Chandrasekaran, chairman of Tata Sons (the holding company that controls the Tata Group), announced on August 12 that he would not seek reappointment past February 2027, ending months of uncertainty after a Tata Trusts board member blocked his renewal. Markets read leadership uncertainty at India's largest conglomerate as a risk, since Tata companies span everything from software to steel to cars.

stories.title: India says it is 'examining' Bangladesh's renewed request to extradite Sheikh Hasina
stories.what_happened: India's government said it is **'examining' Bangladesh's request for the extradition of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina** in line with established legal processes, responding a day after Bangladesh's interim leadership renewed its extradition demand during a meeting between India's High Commissioner, Dinesh Trivedi, and Bangladesh's Prime Minister, Tarique Rahman. This marks the **third official extradition request** Dhaka has sent since Hasina fled to India two years ago. Hasina, 78, was convicted by Bangladesh's special International Crimes Tribunal on charges of crimes against humanity related to the deadly 2024 protest crackdown and sentenced to death in November. India's statement stops short of any commitment on timing or outcome, keeping the request under review rather than acting on it.
key_points: India says it is **'examining'** Bangladesh's latest formal request to extradite **Sheikh Hasina** through established legal channels.
This is the **third official extradition request** Dhaka has sent since Hasina fled to India in August 2024.
Hasina, now 78, was **convicted and sentenced to death** in November by a special tribunal in Dhaka for crimes against humanity tied to the 2024 protest crackdown.
The statement came a day after **India's High Commissioner met Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman**, where Dhaka renewed its demand.
India has **not committed to a timeline or decision** — 'examining' signals the request is being processed, not approved.

depth.background: Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh's longtime prime minister, fled to India in August 2024 after a student-led uprising forced the collapse of her government amid a violent crackdown on protesters. Bangladesh's interim and subsequent governments have since pursued Hasina through Dhaka's International Crimes Tribunal (ICT), and in November she was convicted in absentia of **crimes against humanity** and sentenced to death over her government's response to the 2024 protests. India and Bangladesh have a bilateral extradition treaty, but India has so far neither granted nor formally rejected Dhaka's earlier requests, leaving Hasina's status in India in diplomatic limbo for close to two years.

thread.previously: We reported that Bangladesh's interim government had renewed pressure on India to extradite ousted former PM Sheikh Hasina, who has been living in India since fleeing Dhaka in 2024.
thread.changed: India has now given its first substantive response, saying it is **'examining' the extradition request** through established legal processes — a meeting between India's High Commissioner and Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman preceded the statement. This is Dhaka's **third formal extradition request** since Hasina fled.

stories.title: Root scraps England's midnight curfew in his first move as reinstated Test captain
stories.what_happened: Root confirmed England will not operate under a curfew for the upcoming three-match Test series against Pakistan, arguing that if players are trusted to make good decisions on the field, they should be trusted to do the same off it. It's the first real decision of his reinstated captaincy, and directly reverses the disciplinary approach that led to Stokes and Atkinson's suspension earlier in the year. The series begins August 19.
key_points: Joe Root has **abolished England's midnight curfew** ahead of the Pakistan Test series.
It's his **first concrete decision** since being reinstated as Test captain.
Root says players should be trusted to **manage themselves like adults** off the field, just as they are on it.
The curfew is the same rule **Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson were suspended for breaching** earlier this year.
The three-match series against Pakistan begins **August 19**.

depth.background: England's Test set-up has been through turbulence this year: Ben Stokes retired in June during the New Zealand series, having earlier been suspended for a Test — along with pace bowler Gus Atkinson — for breaching the team's midnight curfew during a night out. Former coach Brendon McCullum also stepped down after England lost that series 2-1. Root, England's most-capped modern batter, has now returned to the Test captaincy he previously held, alongside a new coaching setup.

stories.title: Lok Sabha sends contested FCRA bill, which lets the government seize NGOs' foreign-funded assets, to a joint panel
stories.what_happened: On Wednesday, the government moved a motion to send the bill to a joint committee of both Houses rather than push it through for a final vote, after weeks of protest from the Opposition and civil society groups. The motion passed amid an Opposition uproar, with Congress, the Samajwadi Party and others demanding the bill be scrapped entirely rather than merely reviewed. The 31-member committee must submit its report by the last day of the first week of Parliament's Winter Session. At the bill's core is the new Designated Authority, which can take **provisional and then permanent control** of the money and property of any organisation that loses its FCRA registration, and then sell those assets — though it is barred from altering the religious character of a place of worship bought with foreign funds. The government says the changes close loopholes and tighten oversight of overseas money entering India; critics, including some foreign observers per earlier reporting, call it a tool to squeeze NGOs, churches and rights groups the state dislikes.
key_points: The Lok Sabha today passed a motion referring the **Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026** to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) for detailed review instead of a straight vote.
The JPC will have **31 members** — 21 from the Lok Sabha, 10 from the Rajya Sabha — and must report back by the first week of the **Winter Session**.
The bill creates a new **'Designated Authority'** that can take over and sell the assets of NGOs whose foreign-funding licence is cancelled, surrendered, or not renewed.
Congress's **Shashi Tharoor** and other opposition leaders say the bill hands government sweeping power over civil society; the **Kerala Assembly** has passed a resolution demanding it be withdrawn.
Proceeds from any sale of seized assets would go straight into the **Consolidated Fund of India**, the government's main account.

depth.background: The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, or **FCRA**, has governed how Indian NGOs, charities, and religious and educational institutions receive money from abroad since **2010**, requiring every recipient to register and report the funds. Union Minister of State for Home Affairs **Nityanand Rai** introduced this amendment bill in the Lok Sabha back in **March 2026** on behalf of Home Minister Amit Shah, and it has drawn sustained pushback since — from churches and missionary groups to international rights bodies — over how much control it gives the state.

stories.title: England opener Emilio Gay named in warm-up squad ahead of Pakistan Tests, easing shoulder-injury fears
stories.what_happened: On **August 7**, while batting for Durham against Middlesex in a one-day match, Gay first felt discomfort in his right shoulder, then aggravated it two overs later hitting a boundary; he immediately called for the physio and retired hurt on 9 off 17 balls, undergoing a scan over the following days. Despite that scare, Gay has now been named in the **PCC Select XI** — a first-class invitational team — for a three-day tour match against Pakistan starting **August 13** at Beckenham, Kent's ground. Sky Sports reported it understands Gay is expected to be fit for the Test series, and his inclusion in this squad is the clearest sign yet that the shoulder issue isn't ruling him out of the opener at Headingley on **August 19**.
key_points: England Test opener **Emilio Gay** was named in the 14-player **PCC Select XI** for a three-day warm-up match against touring Pakistan, starting **August 13 at Beckenham**.
Gay had retired hurt on **9 off 17 balls** on **August 7**, clutching his shoulder while batting for Durham, after aggravating discomfort that began two overs earlier.
His selection suggests he's expected to prove fitness in time for the **first Test at Headingley on August 19**, the opener of a three-match series against Pakistan.
The squad is captained by **Tom Haines** and includes uncapped and fringe players like Shoaib Bashir and Josh Hull.
A lost place for Gay would have forced England to reshuffle its top order just days before a marquee home series.

depth.background: Gay only nailed down England's Test opening slot earlier this year, making his fitness a genuine selection question rather than a formality. The warm-up match against Pakistan's touring side is the traditional final fitness and form check before a Test series — Pakistan's three-Test tour runs Headingley (Aug 19), Lord's (Aug 27-31) and Edgbaston (Sept 9-13).

stories.title: Ukraine hits Russia's last safe Black Sea Fleet harbor at Novorossiysk, damaging four warships
stories.what_happened: Overnight on **August 12**, Ukraine's military carried out what President Zelensky called a 'unique operation' against the naval base at Novorossiysk, more than **300 kilometers** from the nearest front line. Ukrainian forces combined **Palianytsia jet-powered attack drones**, Neptune anti-ship cruise missiles, and uncrewed naval drones in the strike. Four Russian warships were damaged: the frigates **Admiral Makarov** and **Admiral Essen**, the missile ship **Buyan-M**, and the patrol ship **Vasily Bykov**. The strike also hit an S-300 air-defense radar protecting the port and the **Sheskharis oil terminal**, a major crude-export point, along with infrastructure across several piers. Russian officials have not published a detailed damage assessment.
key_points: **Four Russian warships** were damaged — two frigates (Admiral Makarov, Admiral Essen), a missile ship (Buyan-M), and a patrol ship (Vasily Bykov).
Novorossiysk sits more than **300 kilometers** from the front line and had become Russia's main safe harbor after Crimea's ports were made too dangerous.
Ukraine combined **Palianytsia jet-powered drones**, Neptune cruise missiles, and naval drones in the strike — a mix it couldn't field a few years ago.
The attack also hit the **Sheskharis oil terminal**, one of Russia's largest crude-export points, and an S-300 air-defense radar guarding the base.
President Zelensky called it a **'unique operation'** targeting what was left of Russia's Black Sea safe harbor.

depth.background: Novorossiysk, on Russia's Black Sea coast, became the main home of the **Black Sea Fleet** after two years of Ukrainian missile and drone strikes made Crimean ports like Sevastopol too dangerous to anchor in. The port does double duty as one of Russia's biggest oil-export terminals, moving crude that arrives via pipeline from deep inland. Through 2026, Ukraine has steadily extended the range and reliability of its domestically built long-range drones and missiles, pushing further from the front line than it could a year or two ago. This strike is the latest sign that no Russian Black Sea harbor is now truly out of reach.

stories.title: Parliamentary panel finds all three charges proved against ex-judge Yashwant Varma in the cash-at-residence case
stories.what_happened: The parliamentary inquiry committee — Justice Aravind Kumar, former Bombay High Court Chief Justice Shree Chandrashekhar, and senior advocate B.V. Acharya — tabled its **126-page report** in both houses of Parliament on **August 12**, finding **all three charges against Varma proved**: unexplained possession of large amounts of cash at his official residence, failure to preserve evidence after the fire, and giving misleading explanations for the money's presence. The committee did not go so far as to conclude that Varma personally owned or tried to remove the cash himself, leaving a key factual question about intent unresolved. Varma had already resigned from the judiciary in April 2026, before the report's findings were made public, while continuing to deny any wrongdoing. It remains unclear whether Parliament will now pursue a formal impeachment motion, since Varma is no longer a sitting judge.
key_points: A three-member parliamentary committee found **all three charges proved** against former judge **Yashwant Varma** in the cash-at-residence case.
The charges: **unexplained possession of large amounts of cash**, failure to preserve evidence, and misleading explanations for the money.
Officials found the cash at Varma's official Delhi residence after a **fire in March 2025** — he denies the money was his.
The **126-page report** was tabled in both houses of Parliament; Varma had already **resigned from the judiciary in April 2026**.
The panel **stopped short** of concluding Varma personally owned or removed the money, leaving the question of intent unresolved.

depth.background: In March 2025, a fire broke out at the official Delhi residence of Justice Yashwant Varma, then a sitting judge, and firefighters reportedly discovered large sacks of half-burnt currency notes on the property. The discovery triggered a major scandal about judicial accountability, since sitting judges in India enjoy strong protections against ordinary criminal investigation — removing one requires a Parliament-driven, impeachment-style process. A three-member committee, made up of a Supreme Court judge, a former High Court chief justice, and a senior advocate, was set up to investigate. Varma resigned from the judiciary in April 2026 while maintaining he had done nothing wrong.

stories.title: US inflation cools slightly in July, but the Fed still isn't ready to cut rates
stories.what_happened: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on **August 12** that the Consumer Price Index rose **0.1%** in July after actually falling 0.4% in June, a reversal that still left the **annual rate at 3.4%**, down slightly from the prior month. Core CPI — the Fed's preferred gauge because it excludes volatile food and energy prices — climbed 0.2% for the month, with its annual pace **easing to 2.5%**. Shelter, which makes up roughly a third of the entire index, rose 0.1% and alone accounted for about two-thirds of July's overall increase. Energy prices provided relief, dropping 1.5% after a steep 5.7% fall in June. Markets initially cheered the report as evidence inflation isn't reaccelerating: the S&P 500 climbed about 0.26% to close at 7,748.50 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.54% to 26,588.49, helped along by AI-linked stocks. But traders' bets on a Fed rate cut in September stayed muted, since inflation remains well above the 2% target.
key_points: Headline US consumer prices rose just **0.1%** in July, holding the annual inflation rate at **3.4%**
**Core inflation** (which strips out food and energy) rose 0.2% for the month; its annual rate eased to **2.5%**
**Shelter costs** — rent and housing — drove roughly two-thirds of July's price increase on their own
Energy prices fell **1.5%** in July, cushioning the headline number after a 5.7% drop in June
Wall Street read it as good-but-not-great news: the **S&P 500** and Nasdaq both edged higher, but traders still see little chance of a Fed rate cut this year

depth.background: The US Federal Reserve targets **2% annual inflation** as the sweet spot for a healthy economy — enough price growth to signal demand, not so much that it erodes paychecks. Since 2025, inflation has stayed stubbornly above that target, kept elevated by tariffs on imported goods, high shelter costs, and a resilient job market that keeps consumer spending strong. The monthly **Consumer Price Index (CPI)**, published by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, is the single most-watched number for figuring out what the Fed will do next with interest rates — the cost of borrowing money that ripples through mortgages, credit cards, and business loans worldwide.

stories.title: US inflation comes in roughly as expected, and stocks jump as traders bet the Fed will cut rates next month
stories.what_happened: The Bureau of Labor Statistics released the July **Consumer Price Index (CPI)** report at 8:30am ET on August 12. Headline inflation rose **0.2%** from June to July and **2.7%** year-over-year — a hair below the 2.7-2.8% range economists had expected, and cooler than June's pace. **Core CPI**, which strips out volatile food and energy prices to show the underlying trend, rose 0.3% month-over-month and **3.1%** year-over-year, a touch hotter than forecast. Wall Street read the mixed report as 'good enough' to keep the door open for a rate cut: the **Dow Jones rose 1.13%**, the S&P 500 gained 0.72%, and the Nasdaq climbed 0.64%, with the AI trade among the biggest gainers. Futures markets pushed the implied probability of a **quarter- or half-point rate cut** at the Fed's September meeting up to **95%**, from 88% just two days before.
key_points: July's headline inflation rose **2.7%** over the past year, slightly below forecasts.
Core inflation (strips out food and energy) came in a touch hotter at **3.1%** year-on-year.
The **Dow jumped 1.13%**, the S&P 500 rose 0.72%, and the Nasdaq gained 0.64% on the news.
Odds of a **rate cut at the Fed's September 16–17 meeting** jumped to **95%**, from 88% two days earlier.
It's the report investors have been most anxious about all month, given a recent run of weak US jobs data.

depth.background: The Consumer Price Index, or **CPI**, is the US government's main measure of how fast the price of everyday goods and services is rising — it's what people mean when they say 'inflation'. The Federal Reserve, America's central bank, is supposed to keep inflation near 2% while also keeping unemployment low; when inflation is too hot, the Fed keeps interest rates high to cool the economy down, which makes borrowing (mortgages, credit cards, business loans) more expensive. Going into today, weak US hiring data had already pushed traders to bet the Fed would start cutting rates soon, and this report was seen as the last big test of that bet before the Fed's next meeting.

stories.title: Russia releases US Marine veteran Robert Gilman after nearly four years in detention, on Trump's personal appeal to Putin
stories.what_happened: Russia released Gilman on what officials describe as humanitarian grounds, and he has now arrived back in the United States. His advocates say that before his release he had been in a dissociative stupor for 47 days as a result of alleged physical and psychological abuse in custody, and had to be moved to a hospital, hooked to a feeding tube and handcuffed to a bed. Trump said he personally discussed the case with Vladimir Putin and that Russia agreed to free Gilman without asking for anyone in return — a departure from the more typical prisoner-swap pattern seen in past releases. Gilman is now traveling to a US military hospital in Texas, where he'll undergo medical and psychological evaluation before any further treatment.
key_points: **Robert Gilman**, a 32-year-old former US Marine, has been released from Russian detention and has returned to the United States.
He was held since **2022** on disputed charges of beating a police officer after being pulled off a train for causing a disturbance.
His family and advocates say he was tortured, and was in a **'dissociative stupor' for 47 days** before being moved to a hospital.
President **Trump personally raised the case with Putin**, and says Russia asked for **nothing in return** — no prisoner swap took place.
Gilman is headed to a **US military hospital in Texas** for medical and psychological assessment.

depth.background: Gilman was detained in Russia in 2022, one of a number of Americans caught up in Russian legal proceedings since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began that year. Such cases have often become bargaining chips: past releases, like the 2024 multi-country prisoner exchange, involved Russia swapping detained Americans for Russians held in Western countries. Gilman's family and legal advocates have spent years arguing his charges were disputed and that he was being mistreated in custody, warning at points that he was near death.

stories.title: Fernando Alonso set to extend his Aston Martin contract through 2027-28, demanding a big pay rise
stories.what_happened: According to multiple reports this week, Alonso and Aston Martin have moved toward agreeing a contract extension that would keep him with the team through 2027, and possibly 2028. Alonso is said to be pushing hard in negotiations, demanding close to a 33% salary increase that would take his annual pay to around €40 million. People close to the team expect the new deal could be formally announced as soon as the Dutch Grand Prix weekend at Zandvoort, later this month. Team principal Adrian Newey said he is confident the partnership will continue, and Alonso himself has downplayed the exit speculation, saying plainly that he has a contract and isn't planning to switch teams — though he has left open exactly which season(s) he'll commit to as a driver.
key_points: Alonso is reportedly set to **stay at Aston Martin**, agreeing terms on a new deal covering **2027 and possibly 2028**.
He's said to be demanding around a **33% pay rise**, pushing his annual salary toward roughly **€40 million**.
The deal could be **announced as early as the Dutch Grand Prix** at Zandvoort (August 21-23).
Team boss **Adrian Newey** says he's 'pretty confident' the Alonso relationship continues.
Alonso himself put it simply: **'I have a contract, I'm not going to change teams.'**

depth.background: Fernando Alonso, F1's most experienced active driver, has been at Aston Martin since 2023, helping build the team into a more competitive outfit alongside major investment from owner Lawrence Stroll. Alonso's existing contract has performance-linked exit conditions, and heading into this month there had been real uncertainty about his future — team owner Stroll had publicly named Carlos Sainz as his 'top candidate' to replace Alonso if he left, and rumors swirled of a possible Alonso move to Alpine for 2027.

stories.title: ICC's chief executive says the era of randomly scheduled cricket series 'has to come to an end'
stories.what_happened: In comments published today, Gupta directly criticized the current model of "randomly scheduled bilateral series," saying countries won't be able to keep funding cricket without matches that carry real context and competitive stakes. He argued the sport needs series built around "context, culture, competition and competitiveness" rather than fixtures scheduled mainly for broadcast revenue. He also defended the **ODI format** specifically, saying it remains "inextricably linked" to the men's and women's World Cups and can thrive rather than just survive. His remarks come as the ICC prepares to finalize its next Future Tours Programme, covering **2027 to 2031**, at meetings in Hong Kong later this year — a cycle that opens with the **2027 Men's Cricket World Cup** across South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.
key_points: ICC CEO **Sanjog Gupta** said bilateral cricket series scheduled without context or stakes "**has to come to an end**," warning countries can't sustain cricket without competition behind it.
He named four pillars series need to hold attention: "**context, culture, competition and competitiveness**."
On the **ODI format**, long debated as dying, Gupta said it can "**continue not just to survive, but thrive**," tying it closely to the men's and women's World Cups.
The comments come ahead of ICC meetings in **Hong Kong later in 2026**, where the next Future Tours Programme, covering **2027-2031**, will be finalized.
The **2027 Men's World Cup**, co-hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, will be the first event of that new scheduling cycle.

depth.background: Cricket boards outside the "Big Three" of India, Australia and England have struggled for years to finance bilateral tours that carry no real stakes — no league table, no qualification consequence — while fans and broadcasters increasingly tune out matches that don't matter. Gupta, a former broadcasting executive who became ICC CEO in 2025, has been signaling a shift toward more structured, context-driven formats since taking the role.

stories.title: xAI ships Grok 4.6, matching GPT-5.6 as the AI model race keeps accelerating
stories.what_happened: xAI released **Grok 4.6** on August 12 as the direct successor to Grok 4.5, available immediately through its API, the Cursor code editor, and its own Grok Build environment. Rather than making the model bigger, xAI kept the same 1.5-trillion-parameter foundation and improved it through better fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, plus an expanded **500,000-token context window** for handling large codebases or documents in one go. On xAI's own benchmark table, Grok 4.6 scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index in its high-reasoning mode, up from 56 for Grok 4.5, putting it roughly level with GPT-5.6 Sol Max. It bills at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens for shorter prompts, which xAI is marketing as roughly half the price of comparable frontier models. A larger 2.1-trillion-parameter Grok 4.7 is reportedly planned for release a few weeks later.
key_points: xAI (under SpaceXAI) launched **Grok 4.6**, its newest flagship AI model, on **August 12**
It scores **61** on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, up from 56 for Grok 4.5
That ties it with **GPT-5.6 Sol Max** for third-best in the world on that benchmark
It has a **500,000-token context window**, letting developers feed it entire codebases at once
Pricing stays at **$2/$6 per million tokens** in/out — roughly half the price of some rival models

depth.background: The large AI-model industry has settled into a rapid release cadence, with OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and xAI each pushing out upgraded flagship models every few months to stay ahead on independent benchmarks like the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. xAI, Elon Musk's AI company (now folded under the SpaceXAI banner), has been racing to close the gap with better-funded rivals, leaning on cheaper pricing and long-context, coding-focused features to win developers. Grok 4.5, its predecessor, trailed the top tier of models on most independent benchmarks.

stories.title: Monsoon turns deadly in central India as IMD widens its rain alert to 19 states
stories.what_happened: On Monday, a van carrying 11 people — three men, four women and four children — drove onto a flooded, under-construction bridge over the Jhiri drain near Padana village in Rajgarh despite warnings from locals and officials not to cross; the current swept the vehicle away and it sank within moments, killing 9 of the occupants, with a search continuing for the last person. The next day, Bhopal was hit by 74.5mm of rain in just three hours, flooding over 1,000 homes and forcing State Disaster Response Force teams and Home Guards to rescue 98 people and a number of stranded animals. Rajasthan's Jhalawar district recorded the state's heaviest rainfall of the season, around 300mm, swelling the Kalisindh and Ahu rivers enough to cut off roughly 10 villages and strand pilgrims near a riverside temple. Today the IMD extended its alert further, warning of heavy to very heavy rain and storms across 19 states, from Jammu & Kashmir and Uttarakhand — where all 12 districts are under a flash-flood warning — down toward the south.
key_points: The **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** issued fresh heavy-rain and thunderstorm warnings for **19 states** today, including Delhi-NCR, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Rajasthan, with gusts up to **90 km/h**.

In Madhya Pradesh's **Rajgarh district**, a van carrying 11 people was swept into a flooded drain on Monday; **9 people, including 3 children, died**, and a search continues for the last missing passenger.
**Bhopal** recorded 74.5mm of rain in three hours, flooding more than **1,000 homes** and forcing rescuers to save 98 people and several animals.
Rajasthan's Jhalawar district received about **300mm (roughly 12 inches)** of rain, the state's heaviest this season, triggering an orange alert in six districts and shutting schools.
Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister **Mohan Yadav** announced ₹4 lakh in compensation for each family that lost a member in the Rajgarh tragedy.

depth.background: India's four-month monsoon season (June–September) delivers roughly 70% of the country's annual rainfall and is essential for farming, but it also triggers floods, landslides and flash floods almost every year — and this year has already been especially deadly, with **Himachal Pradesh** alone recording 157 deaths from floods and landslides. This week the crisis has widened into central India, with **Madhya Pradesh** and **Rajasthan** bearing the brunt of intense, localised downpours.

stories.title: Russia is now importing gasoline refined in India from its own crude — a sign its refineries are buckling under drone strikes
stories.what_happened: Tracking firm Kpler confirmed that a Russian-flagged tanker carrying **42,000 metric tons** of gasoline arrived at a Russian port on **Aug. 5**, having loaded the fuel in mid-June at Nayara Energy's Vadinar refinery in Gujarat, India, and transferred it via an Omani-flagged carrier in Egypt en route. Nayara is roughly **49% owned by Rosneft**. The shipment amounts to Russia importing gasoline made from its own crude oil, refined abroad, because Ukrainian drone strikes have cut its domestic refining capacity to a **21-year low** — refinery throughput ran at 3.6 million barrels a day in July, more than 30% below the seasonal average — creating a real domestic fuel shortage inside Russia.
key_points: A tanker carrying **42,000 metric tons** of gasoline refined at an Indian refinery has arrived in Russia — a reversal of Russia's usual role as a fuel exporter.
Ukrainian drone strikes have pushed Russian refining capacity to a **21-year low**, over **30% below** its seasonal average in July.
The gasoline came from **Nayara Energy's Vadinar refinery** in Gujarat, which is **49% owned by Russia's Rosneft**.
The fuel was routed through an **Omani-flagged carrier** in Egypt, obscuring the direct India-to-Russia link.
It's essentially Russian crude oil, refined in India, being **shipped back to Russia** because Russia can no longer refine enough of it domestically.

depth.background: Since the EU sanctioned much of Russia's oil trade following its invasion of Ukraine, discounted Russian crude has become a major feedstock for refiners willing to buy it, including **Nayara Energy** — an Indian refinery operator roughly half-owned by Russia's state oil giant **Rosneft**. Nayara has increasingly relied on Russian crude as Western suppliers stayed away, and typically sells its refined output through third-party traders rather than direct transactions, which is how fuel with Russian origins can end up back in Russia without registering as a formal government-to-government deal. Meanwhile, Ukraine has spent much of 2026 striking Russian oil refineries with long-range drones, aiming to cripple Moscow's ability to fuel its own economy and military.

stories.title: Mercedes admits grid penalties for Antonelli and Russell are 'almost inevitable' in F1's second half
stories.what_happened: Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord confirmed that grid penalties are now close to unavoidable for both Kimi Antonelli and George Russell in the second half of the 2026 season, telling reporters: "I think, looking at how many we've used in the first half of the season, it's almost inevitable that at some point there will be penalties to take." Both drivers are already on their **fourth ICE and fourth exhaust** — the maximum allowed before a mandatory grid-drop applies to any further change. Team principal Toto Wolff said he still hopes a penalty can be avoided, but is already planning where to take one if necessary, floating the Italian Grand Prix at **Monza** as the preferred venue because its long straights make it the easiest track on the calendar to recover lost grid positions. The timing matters because Mercedes currently leads the constructors' championship by **72 points** at the summer break, and Antonelli holds a **50-point** cushion in the drivers' standings — a lead built on the strength of what's been the fastest car of the season, even as reliability issues have repeatedly threatened it.
key_points: Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord said penalties are **'almost inevitable'** for title contenders **Kimi Antonelli and George Russell**.
Both drivers are already on their **fourth engine and exhaust** — the maximum allowed before an automatic grid-drop penalty kicks in.
Antonelli leads the drivers' championship by **50 points**; Mercedes leads the constructors' standings by **72 points** at the summer break.
Team boss Toto Wolff is already eyeing **Monza's long straights** as the easiest track to absorb a penalty and recover lost places.
Mercedes has been the year's fastest car, but **reliability, not pace**, has been its main weakness.

depth.background: In Formula 1, each car is allowed a limited number of engine and exhaust changes per season before a driver is automatically hit with a grid-position penalty for using an extra one. Mercedes has dominated on pace this season, but has burned through engine components faster than planned — Antonelli's fourth internal combustion engine and exhaust went in during the Belgian Grand Prix after a suspected fault was found in his previous unit, while Russell's fourth engine followed a cracked oil sump discovered during Hungarian GP qualifying. With both drivers already at the four-unit ceiling, any further swap this season would trigger a penalty.

stories.title: DR Congo's Ebola death toll climbs to 2,128 and cases pass 4,500, confirming it as the fastest-growing outbreak on record
stories.what_happened: Health authorities reported that, as of data through August 11, the outbreak has grown to **4,566 confirmed cases and 2,128 deaths**, an increase of 117 cases and 67 deaths in just one day. The virus is now present in **53 of the country's 140 health zones** across five provinces, and 570 patients are currently hospitalised in isolation units. Officials and UN reporting describe this as the **fastest-growing Ebola outbreak DR Congo has ever recorded**, and in total scale it is now second only to the devastating 2014–2016 West African epidemic that killed over 11,000 people across multiple countries. UN News separately reported that many patients in remote areas are dying before they can even reach a doctor, underscoring how thin the region's health infrastructure is.
key_points: Deaths have risen to **2,128**, with **4,566 confirmed cases** across five provinces of DR Congo.
**117 new cases and 67 new deaths** were reported in a single day, showing the outbreak is still accelerating.
It is now officially the **fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record**, and the second-deadliest ever after the 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic.
**570 patients** are currently hospitalised in isolation as the outbreak spreads to 53 of the country's 140 health zones.
UN officials say many victims are **dying before they ever reach a doctor**, pointing to a collapsed rural health system.

depth.background: This is the **Bundibugyo virus** strain of Ebola, first identified in this outbreak in DR Congo's Ituri province earlier in 2026 before spreading to North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo and Haut-Uele provinces — a region already strained by armed conflict and weak infrastructure. Ebola is a severe, often fatal viral disease spread through contact with bodily fluids of infected people or animals; past outbreaks have been contained through rapid isolation, contact tracing, and (for some strains) vaccination, but DR Congo's mix of conflict, distrust of health workers, and remote terrain has repeatedly made containment difficult. The outbreak was already the deadliest on record in the country as of yesterday, when deaths passed 2,000.

thread.previously: We reported yesterday that the outbreak's death toll had just passed 2,000, spread across five provinces, making it the deadliest Ebola outbreak in DR Congo's history.
thread.changed: New WHO-linked data now puts the toll at **4,566 confirmed cases and 2,128 deaths** — a jump of 117 new cases and 67 new deaths in a single day — with 570 patients currently hospitalised in isolation across 53 of the country's 140 health zones. Health officials are now calling it the **fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record**, and second in total size only to the 2014–2016 West African outbreak that killed over 11,000 people.
