stories.title: Putin threatens to seize European ships 'anywhere' in retaliation for EU moves against Russia's sanctioned 'shadow fleet'
stories.what_happened: President Vladimir Putin said Wednesday that Russia would seize European ships in retaliation if EU countries follow through on selling off cargo from detained Russian 'shadow fleet' tankers. Speaking while overseeing **naval drills in Russia's Far East**, Putin called the EU's sanctions move **'piracy and banditry'** and said, **'We will be forced to respond in kind.'** He specified the retaliation would not necessarily target ships in the same waters where Russian vessels were seized — Russia would act **'anywhere, including in the area of responsibility of the Pacific Fleet.'** The trigger was a new EU sanctions package passed last month permitting member states to sell the oil or cargo seized from shadow-fleet tankers; **nine** such tankers have been detained across Europe since the start of 2026, **four of them by France** alone.
key_points: Putin called EU plans to sell off cargo from seized Russian tankers **'piracy and banditry'** and vowed to **'respond in kind'**.
He said Russia would seize European ships **wherever it 'deems necessary'** — explicitly including the **Pacific**, far from European waters.
The threat responds to new EU sanctions letting member states **sell the oil and cargo** from detained 'shadow fleet' tankers.
**Nine** such tankers have been detained in Europe since the start of 2026, **four of them in France**.
Putin made the comments while personally overseeing **Russian naval drills** in the Far East.

depth.background: Russia's 'shadow fleet' is a network of aging, often unregistered or falsely-flagged oil tankers that Moscow uses to keep exporting oil despite Western **sanctions** imposed after its invasion of Ukraine — sanctions being economic penalties, like trade or financial restrictions, meant to pressure a country's government. European countries have increasingly intercepted and detained these tankers, several of them linked to sanctioned Russian companies or suspected of sabotage, like the tanker that sank off Oman spilling oil across protected coastline. Last month the EU passed new rules letting member states go a step further: not just detain the ships, but actually sell their oil and cargo.

stories.title: Ashwin picks his India squad for the 2027 ODI World Cup — and leaves out Pant, Samson and Shami
stories.what_happened: Ashwin used his platform to name his personal 15-man India squad for the **2027 ODI World Cup**, more than a year out from the tournament. His most notable call was backing a **return for Bhuvneshwar Kumar**, saying: **'Kumar is a yes. I would communicate and ask him to play all the first-class tournaments to make sure he is ready and primed to go to South Africa.'** He named **Kuldeep Yadav** as his first-choice spinner, with **Harshit Rana, Mohammed Siraj and Jasprit Bumrah** rounding out his pace attack, and listed **Shubman Gill, Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli** as certainties. The bigger talking point was who he **left out**: **Rishabh Pant, Sanju Samson, Mohammed Shami, Washington Sundar**, along with younger names like Vaibhav Suryavanshi, Abhishek Sharma, Ravi Bishnoi, Shivam Dube and others.
key_points: Former India spinner **Ravichandran Ashwin** named his personal picks for India's 2027 ODI World Cup squad.
He backs **Bhuvneshwar Kumar's** return, saying the pacer should play domestic first-class cricket to stay 'primed' for selection.
Big names left out include **Rishabh Pant, Sanju Samson, Mohammed Shami, Washington Sundar**, and several young players.
**Kuldeep Yadav** is his first-choice spinner, with **Harshit Rana, Mohammed Siraj and Jasprit Bumrah** as his pace picks.
**Shubman Gill, Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli** are named as his 'early certainties' for the squad.

depth.background: The next 50-over **ODI World Cup** is scheduled for **2027 in South Africa**, still more than a year away, which is exactly why pundit squad predictions like this one get attention — they're an early read on how India's selectors might be thinking about form, fitness, and roles. Ashwin, one of India's most successful bowlers before retiring from international cricket, is now a prominent TV and YouTube analyst whose picks carry weight because of his insider experience with India's set-up and selection debates.

stories.title: Sussex all-rounder Danny Lamb forced into retirement at 30 after career-ending neck injury
stories.what_happened: Lamb sustained a **disc herniation** in his neck during play this season, which led to a **spinal cord injury** — a serious condition that can affect strength, sensation and movement. Last month he had **urgent neck discectomy and fusion surgery**, a procedure that removes the damaged disc and fuses the surrounding vertebrae to stabilise the spine. Despite the operation, the lingering effects of the injury mean doctors have advised him not to continue playing professional cricket, and Lamb announced his retirement on **12 August 2026** at age 30. He leaves the game having played **38 First-Class, 34 List A and 82 T20 matches**, taking five-wicket hauls in every format.
key_points: **Danny Lamb**, the Sussex all-rounder, has retired from professional cricket at just **30 years old** on medical advice.
He suffered a **disc herniation** in his neck earlier this season that caused a **spinal cord injury**.
Lamb underwent **neck discectomy and fusion surgery** last month but has not recovered enough to keep playing.
Across his career he took **208 First-Class wickets** and scored **4,232 First-Class runs** for Lancashire and Sussex.
He was central to Sussex's **promotion to Division One** of the County Championship and their 2024 Vitality Blast Finals Day run.

depth.background: Lamb came through the ranks at **Lancashire** before moving to the south coast to join **Sussex** in 2023, quickly becoming a key all-rounder for the club with both bat and ball. In 2024 he was a driving force behind Sussex's promotion back to **Division One** of the County Championship, scoring 375 runs and taking 13 wickets that campaign, and also helped the side reach Finals Day in the T20 Vitality Blast. Earlier this season he suffered a serious neck injury that damaged his spinal cord, forcing him out of action and eventually onto the operating table.

stories.title: India moves a step closer to owning fighter-jet engine technology, as the Safran-GTRE deal for its stealth jet nears final government approval
stories.what_happened: A joint venture proposal between **Safran** and **DRDO's GTRE** is nearing final approval from India's **Cabinet Committee on Security**, with clearance expected **ahead of August 15**. Once approved, it will allow the two sides to open **final negotiations** and sign a formal cooperation contract. The deal covers a new turbofan engine in the **110–130 kN thrust class**, built specifically to power the **AMCA Mark-2**, the more advanced stealth version of India's homegrown fighter jet. The engine is planned to start at **120 kN** of thrust with a later **140 kN** uprated version, and the program calls for **nine prototype engines** to be built and certified. Officials and defence analysts describe the deal's biggest significance as intellectual property: for the first time, India would **own the full IP** for an advanced fighter engine, rather than licensing or importing the technology.
key_points: The Safran-GTRE joint venture to build the engine for India's **AMCA Mark-2** stealth fighter is nearing approval from India's top security body, the **CCS**.
Clearance is expected **before August 15**, India's Independence Day.
The engine targets **110–130 kilonewtons (kN)** of thrust — starting at 120 kN, later uprated to **140 kN**.
**Nine prototype engines** are planned to be built and certified under the deal.
This would be the **first time India owns full intellectual property** in an advanced fighter jet engine — something it has never had before.

depth.background: The **AMCA (Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft)** is India's own fifth-generation stealth fighter program, run by defence research body **DRDO**. A long-standing weakness of India's fighter jet ambitions has been engines: India has always had to buy or license foreign engines (from Russia, the US, or France) and has never owned the underlying technology outright. **GTRE (Gas Turbine Research Establishment)**, DRDO's engine-design arm, has partnered with French aerospace giant **Safran** to co-develop a new high-thrust engine specifically for the stealthier AMCA Mark-2 variant. The proposal now needs sign-off from India's **Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS)**, the top government body that approves major defence deals, chaired by the Prime Minister.

stories.title: Cadillac names ex-Alpine chief Marcin Budkowski to replace sacked team boss Graeme Lowdon
stories.what_happened: Cadillac announced that Marcin Budkowski, previously executive director at Alpine and a veteran of senior roles at Prost, Ferrari, McLaren and the FIA, will take over as team principal, replacing Graeme Lowdon. CEO Dan Towriss said the decision was his, and that Lowdon was only informed on Wednesday morning. Cadillac framed the move as a planned transition from the team's 'initial build phase' into 'the next stage of racing performance,' though it had not previously signaled it intended to move on from Lowdon. The change comes a week before the F1 season resumes with the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort.
key_points: Cadillac has appointed **Marcin Budkowski**, formerly Alpine's executive director, as its new F1 team principal.
He replaces **Graeme Lowdon**, who was informed of the decision on **Wednesday morning** and had led the team since its launch.
CEO **Dan Towriss** made the call himself, calling it a 'planned leadership transition' from build phase to performance phase.
Budkowski, 49, has **over two decades in F1** with Prost, Ferrari, McLaren, the FIA, and Renault/Alpine.
The change lands **a week before** the season resumes at the Dutch Grand Prix.

depth.background: Cadillac, backed by General Motors, is Formula 1's newest team, having entered the grid for the 2026 season. Graeme Lowdon played a central role in standing up the team from scratch — securing its F1 entry and building its early operations. A mid-season change of team principal is unusual, especially for a team still in its debut year.

stories.title: Aston Martin's Jessica Hawkins says strength isn't why F1 has no female drivers — the junior ladder is
stories.what_happened: In new comments this week, building on remarks made on the "Road to Success" podcast on **August 10**, Hawkins pushed back on the long-running "are women strong enough for F1" debate, arguing the neck strain she felt in her own F1 test was a universal first-timer challenge, not a gender-specific limit. Instead, she pointed to a specific engineering gap: F1 cars have power steering, but the junior categories, **Formula 2 and Formula 3**, do not — making them physically harder to drive than the F1 cars they're meant to prepare drivers for. She said this disproportionately disadvantages women trying to climb the ladder, since they never even reach F1 machinery. Hawkins reiterated her belief that a woman will race in F1 "within a few years," crediting F1 Academy as the pathway.
key_points: Aston Martin driver ambassador **Jessica Hawkins** rejected the idea that women lack the strength for F1: "**I am absolutely convinced women are strong enough for Formula 1**."
She says the real barrier is **Formula 2 and Formula 3**, the junior categories drivers must climb before F1 — those cars have **no power steering**, making them "notoriously heavy to steer."
Hawkins said F2 is **"a lot more physical than Formula 1 in different areas,"** disproportionately disadvantaging women trying to climb the ladder.
She predicts a woman will race in F1 **"within a few years,"** pointing to the **F1 Academy** — an all-female feeder series launched in 2023 — as the pipeline that will produce that driver.
Hawkins became the **first woman in nearly five years** to drive a modern F1 car when she tested Aston Martin's car in Hungary in 2023.

depth.background: No woman has started a Formula 1 race since the 1970s-80s. F1 Academy was created in **2023** specifically to build a pipeline of female talent through the junior single-seater categories toward F2, F3 and eventually F1. Hawkins, a former W Series racer, is one of the sport's most visible advocates for that pathway.

stories.title: Ferrari has quietly closed the gap on Mercedes heading into F1's summer break, outscoring them in four of the last five races
stories.what_happened: Ferrari has closed the gap on championship leaders Mercedes as the 2026 F1 season heads into its summer break, even though it still trails by **72 points** in the standings. The Italian team has **outscored Mercedes in four of the last five races**, picking up wins at the **Barcelona-Catalunya** and **British Grand Prix**. Central to the turnaround is Ferrari's development record: its **SF-26** is the only car on the entire 2026 grid that hasn't had a single upgrade package rejected — every new part introduced has integrated cleanly and worked as intended, unlike some rivals who have had to pull updates that didn't perform. Ferrari now plans **two more major upgrade packages** for the second half of the season, targeting both **aerodynamics** and the **power unit**, under what the sport calls the ADUO (Additional Development and Update Opportunities) framework, aimed at improving airflow and boosting top-end power on the straights.
key_points: Ferrari trails championship leaders Mercedes by **72 points** heading into the summer break.
But Ferrari has **outscored Mercedes in four of the last five races**, closing what was once a bigger gap.
Ferrari has won at **Barcelona-Catalunya and the British Grand Prix** this season.
Two more major upgrade packages are planned for the second half of 2026, targeting **aerodynamics and the power unit**.
Ferrari's **SF-26** is the only 2026 car that hasn't had a single upgrade package rejected — every update has worked as intended.

depth.background: Formula 1 teams constantly bring new parts — aerodynamic tweaks, engine tuning, floor changes — to their cars throughout a season under the sport's cost-cap and development rules. Not every upgrade works; sometimes a new part actually makes the car slower or unstable and gets pulled. Early in the 2026 season, Mercedes had established itself as the dominant team, with Ferrari the closest challenger but still clearly behind. As the season has progressed toward the summer break — a mid-year pause before racing resumes — the competitive order has been shifting.

stories.title: China calls the India border situation 'generally stable', pushing back on Arunachal face-off reports
stories.what_happened: Asked directly about reports of Chinese military activity near Arunachal Pradesh, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson **Guo Jiakun** said the **'China-India border situation is generally stable at the moment,'** pointing to the **36th round of Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination talks**, held in New Delhi on August 6, where both sides agreed to maintain communication through diplomatic and military channels. It is Beijing's first on-record comment since unverified local reports emerged of Chinese troops entering areas near **Taksing**, roughly **2.5km inside Indian-controlled territory**, before reportedly withdrawing and returning with tents in early August. India's response has been notably firmer: its Ministry of External Affairs has called the state of the border **'most serious'** and said it **'will define'** the broader bilateral relationship, while a separate Indian defence spokesperson called the specific troop-movement claims **'unsubstantiated.'** The two characterizations — India's 'most serious' versus China's 'generally stable' — sit in clear tension even as neither side has escalated militarily.
key_points: Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson **Guo Jiakun** said the **China-India border situation is 'generally stable' at the moment**, responding to questions about reported troop activity near **Arunachal Pradesh**.
This is China's **first on-record response** to reports — which India has called 'unsubstantiated' — of a face-off near **Taksing**, in the Upper Subansiri district.

Guo cited the **36th round of Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination (WMCC) talks** held in New Delhi on **August 6**, where both sides agreed to keep talking through military and diplomatic channels.

China's calmer framing **contrasts with India's**, whose Ministry of External Affairs has called the state of the border 'most serious' and said it **'will define' the wider relationship** with Beijing.

depth.background: Arunachal Pradesh is an Indian state in the eastern Himalayas that China claims in its entirety as 'South Tibet' — one of the two most sensitive stretches of the un-demarcated India-China border, alongside Ladakh in the west, where a deadly 2020 clash killed troops on both sides. Since then, the two countries have cautiously mended ties, including resuming direct flights and border-trade talks, while still holding regular military-to-military talks (the WMCC) to manage day-to-day friction. Unverified reports from local residents in early August claimed Chinese troops had entered areas near Pukar La, Ollo and Taksing in Arunachal's Upper Subansiri district, reportedly withdrawing and then returning to pitch tents — claims neither government has fully confirmed.

thread.previously: India's MEA had called the state of the border 'most serious' and said it 'will define' bilateral ties, while an Indian defence spokesperson separately pushed back harder, calling specific troop-movement claims near Taksing 'unsubstantiated' — without China responding on record.
thread.changed: China's foreign ministry has now responded directly for the first time, with spokesperson Guo Jiakun calling the border situation 'generally stable' and pointing to this month's bilateral talks — a notably calmer characterization than India's.

stories.title: Racing Bulls' surprise climb to 5th in F1's constructors' standings earns a top mid-season grade
stories.what_happened: Motorsport.com's rolling 2026 mid-season grades series, published this week, gave Racing Bulls a **B grade** for what it called an "unprecedented" first half — the team sits **5th in the Constructors' Championship with 66 points**, a position it has never held before. The turning point was a **floor upgrade debuted at the Canadian Grand Prix** (round 5); since then, at least one Racing Bulls car has reached Q3, the final qualifying session, at every subsequent race, and the team has scored double points on five occasions. It sealed 5th place by overtaking a fading **Alpine** at the season's last race before the summer break, the Hungarian Grand Prix. The team achieved this while running a brand-new **Red Bull Ford Powertrains** engine and fielding rookie **Arvid Lindblad** — 2026's only true grid newcomer — alongside **Liam Lawson**, who sits P9 in the Drivers' Championship with 43 points.
key_points: Motorsport.com's mid-season report card gave **Racing Bulls** (Red Bull's sister team) a **B grade**, calling its first half of 2026 "unprecedented."
The team has scored **66 points** — good for an unprecedented **5th place** in the Constructors' Championship at the summer break, ahead of established midfield rivals.
A **floor upgrade introduced in Montreal** (round 5) was the turning point — since then, a Racing Bulls car has reached **Q3 at every round**, with double points scored five times.
Racing Bulls overtook **Alpine** for 5th in the final round before the break, at the Hungarian Grand Prix.
Driver **Liam Lawson** sits **P9 in the Drivers' Championship with 43 points**, leading the midfield pack.

depth.background: Racing Bulls is Red Bull's second, junior F1 team, historically used to develop young drivers rather than fight for constructors' points. **2026 is a full regulation reset** — new chassis and power-unit rules — which scrambled the competitive order; most teams struggled to adapt, but Racing Bulls' aggressive upgrade path let it pull away from rivals like Williams, Haas and Alpine, all of which graded worse in the same mid-season review.

stories.title: 'Lungiwala' remark sparks a privilege motion in the Rajya Sabha as BJP MP denies the charge
stories.what_happened: On **August 10, 2026**, while CPI(M) Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas was speaking, BJP MP Sushmita Dev allegedly left her seat, sat behind him, and repeatedly called him "lungiwala" — a jibe referencing the lungi, a garment stereotypically associated with South Indians. Brittas, who said he was actually wearing a dhoti, filed a formal **privilege motion**, asking that the matter go to the Committee of Privileges for undermining the dignity of the House. The disruption forced Rajya Sabha Chairman C.P. Radhakrishnan to summon both MPs to his chamber, and the House was adjourned until 2 pm. Leader of the House J.P. Nadda told the chamber the BJP does not endorse such remarks but said Dev should get a chance to respond. Today, **August 12**, Dev denied the allegation on record, saying no message from Parliament should divide the country culturally, while stopping short of an apology.
key_points: CPI(M) MP **John Brittas** filed a privilege motion against BJP MP **Sushmita Dev**, accusing her of repeatedly calling him "lungiwala" while he moved a resolution in the **Rajya Sabha on August 10**.
Brittas said he was wearing a **dhoti**, not a lungi, and called the remark a **"deliberate... derogatory stereotype"** about South Indians.
The House was disrupted and briefly **adjourned**; Chairman C.P. Radhakrishnan summoned both MPs to his chamber to resolve the dispute.
Leader of the House **J.P. Nadda** distanced the BJP from the remark, saying "we do not call it lungi; we call it dhoti," while asking that Dev also be heard.
Today, Dev **denied making the remark**, saying "no message from the House should divide India" — without apologizing.

depth.background: The incident happened during a debate on the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill in the Rajya Sabha, as Brittas moved a resolution against a tax ordinance. It taps into a recurring fault line in Indian politics — allegations that Hindi-heartland politicians stereotype South Indian culture — which has flared before over language and revenue-sharing disputes. It's playing out during an already tense **Monsoon Session** dominated by protests, floods, and market shocks.

stories.title: North Korea fires its second ballistic missile in a week, and a missile unit is reportedly heading to Russia
stories.what_happened: South Korea's military detected North Korea launching a ballistic missile from Wonsan in Kangwon province at around **6 a.m. local time on Wednesday, August 12**. Japan's Defense Ministry tracked the missile flying roughly **690 kilometers** and reaching a maximum altitude of about **90 kilometers** before it fell outside Japan's exclusive economic zone, with no reported damage to ships or aircraft. This is North Korea's ninth ballistic missile launch since the start of 2026, and its second in less than a week — the first was a short-range missile fired from the same area on August 6. Separately, South Korean and Western intelligence assessments say a **North Korean missile unit has begun deploying to western Russia**, reportedly equipped with up to 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers that could be used against Ukraine.
key_points: North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the **Sea of Japan** early Wednesday from Wonsan
It flew about **690 km** and reached **90 km** altitude before falling outside Japan's waters
This was Pyongyang's **ninth ballistic missile launch of 2026**, and second in under a week
A North Korean missile unit is reportedly deploying to **western Russia** with up to **120 ballistic missiles**
Seoul says the launches are protest timing against upcoming **US-South Korea military drills**

depth.background: North Korea has ramped up ballistic missile testing through 2026, usually timed to US-South Korea military exercises, which Pyongyang's government treats as rehearsals for an invasion of the North. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, North Korea has become one of Moscow's most important wartime suppliers — first sending artillery shells, then thousands of combat troops, and now reportedly entire missile units. In exchange, analysts believe Kim Jong Un's regime is getting **money, food, and Russian technology transfers** that help modernize North Korea's own weapons programs, including satellite and submarine technology.

stories.title: Gold nears ₹1.55 lakh per 10 grams in India — a record fueled more by the falling rupee than global prices
stories.what_happened: On **Wednesday, August 12**, MCX gold futures rose ₹1,182 to trade around **₹1,54,280 per 10 grams**, with an intraday high of **₹1,54,950** — just short of the ₹1.55 lakh mark and a fresh all-time high in rupee terms. 24-karat gold worked out to roughly **₹15,486 per gram**. Silver moved even more sharply, up ₹2,314 on the day to near **₹2,55,000 per kg**. Internationally, spot gold held around **$4,495/oz** — well below its January 2026 peak of $5,602 — meaning the Indian record reflects rupee depreciation more than fresh global demand. Traders were also watching crude oil, which held near $89/barrel (WTI), and awaiting US inflation data for clues on the Federal Reserve's next rate move.
key_points: MCX gold futures touched an intraday high of **₹1,54,950 per 10 grams** on Wednesday, within reach of the **₹1.55 lakh** mark — a fresh domestic record.
Silver jumped even harder, gaining **₹2,314** on the session to trade near **₹2,55,000 per kg**.

Global spot gold is actually **well below** its all-time high — it peaked at **$5,602/oz in January 2026** and now sits around **$4,495/oz** — so India's record is driven mainly by **rupee weakness**.
The rupee has been sliding as the **Strait of Hormuz standoff** pushes oil prices up, and a weaker rupee mechanically raises the rupee price of gold.
Even as prices hit records, India's jewellery **demand fell about 15% year-on-year** in Q2 2026, per World Gold Council data, as buyers shift to lighter pieces and EMIs.

depth.background: Gold had a historic run in 2026, peaking at **$5,602/oz in January** on central-bank buying and rate-cut bets, before pulling back over 20%. The current push higher in India is layered on top of that — the same Strait of Hormuz crisis rattling oil markets is also weakening the rupee, and because Indian gold prices are set in rupees, currency weakness alone can push them to records even without a global price spike. Gold has long been India's default store of household savings, central to weddings and festivals.

stories.title: A derecho and flash floods kill at least two and cut power to 800,000 across the US Midwest
stories.what_happened: A **derecho** swept across the Midwest and Ohio Valley on **August 11**, spawning at least **six tornadoes**, including three confirmed EF1s in Iowa and three in the Chicago area. Wind gusts reached **160 km/h (99 mph)** at Gary, Indiana, and the storm knocked out power to more than **800,000 customers** across Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky, killing at least **two people**. Overnight, the same system dumped as much as **10 inches (25cm) of rain** on south-central Indiana, and the National Weather Service issued flood warnings for multiple rivers as water levels rose toward major flood stage. Areas near New Castle and Connersville, Indiana, saw close to 10 inches of rain in under 24 hours. Flash flooding swamped homes, vehicles and roads across central Indiana on August 12, with more storms and heavy rain forecast into the evening.
key_points: A **derecho** — a fast-moving line of destructive thunderstorms — tore across the Midwest and Ohio Valley on **August 11**, killing at least **two people**.
More than **800,000 homes and businesses** lost power across Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky.
Winds hit **160 km/h (99 mph)** at Gary, Indiana; at least **six tornadoes** were confirmed or suspected, including three in the Chicago area.
Up to **10 inches (25cm) of rain** fell in south-central Indiana overnight, and forecasters warned of **major river flooding** into Wednesday night.
Flash flood warnings remained active across Indiana on August 12 as rivers continued rising.

depth.background: Derechos are a known but under-the-radar hazard in the US Midwest and Great Plains — long-lived, straight-line windstorms that can damage areas hundreds of miles wide in a single afternoon, unlike a tornado, which is narrow and short-lived. They form when a cluster of thunderstorms organizes around a strong pocket of falling cold air that fans out and accelerates along the ground. **August is peak season** for this kind of storm complex in the Ohio Valley, where warm, humid summer air collides with cooler fronts dropping south from Canada. The region has also had an unusually wet, hot summer, priming rivers and soil for flash flooding when a storm dumps a huge volume of rain in a few hours.

stories.title: Audi's rookie Gabriel Bortoleto is outscoring veteran Nico Hulkenberg 10 points to 2 in its first F1 season
stories.what_happened: Audi's first season as a full F1 works team has produced a mixed but improving picture at the summer break. The team scored points in the season-opening Australian Grand Prix, then went **six consecutive races without adding to its tally**, before a package of car upgrades ahead of the summer break delivered top-10 finishes at **Silverstone, Spa-Francorchamps, and the Hungaroring**. That run puts Audi 8th in the constructors' championship with **12 points** total. The standout is rookie **Gabriel Bortoleto**, who is responsible for **10 of those 12 points**, compared to just 2 for the more experienced **Nico Hulkenberg** — though Hulkenberg still edges Bortoleto in qualifying head-to-head, 6 sessions to 5. **Mattia Binotto**, the former Ferrari team principal, now leads the project as Team Principal following the departure of sporting director Jonathan Wheatley, who had been poached from Red Bull to help build the new works operation.
key_points: **Audi** (the rebranded former Sauber team) has **12 points** in its first season as a full manufacturer works team, sitting 8th in constructors'.
Rookie **Gabriel Bortoleto** has scored **10 of those 12 points**, outperforming veteran teammate **Nico Hulkenberg**.
The team went **six races without scoring** early in the season before upgrades brought top-10 finishes at Silverstone, Spa, and the Hungaroring.
Ex-Ferrari boss **Mattia Binotto** now runs the project as Team Principal, after former Red Bull sporting director **Jonathan Wheatley** departed.
Hulkenberg still leads the **qualifying head-to-head** against Bortoleto, 6 sessions to 5.

depth.background: **Audi** took over the former Sauber team for 2026 to become a full factory 'works' constructor — meaning the car now carries Audi's own power unit and branding rather than running as a customer team, a major and expensive step up in F1. The move was closely watched as a test of whether a new manufacturer entry could compete straight out of the gate against established teams. **Mattia Binotto**, who previously led Ferrari's F1 operation, was brought in to run the project, but the team saw early leadership turbulence when **Jonathan Wheatley**, a respected sporting director poached from Red Bull, departed. Rookie **Gabriel Bortoleto** and experienced campaigner **Nico Hulkenberg** were retained as the driver pairing heading into this transformation.

stories.title: Guenther Steiner says he'd return to F1 — but only for 'a project I like', not just a title
stories.what_happened: Speaking on the 'Up To Speed' podcast with Jolie Sharpe and David Coulthard, Steiner said he would consider coming back to Formula 1 if 'there is a project I like' — explicitly saying he doesn't care about titles. 'A project means something you can shape yourself,' he said. 'I couldn't care less about the job title.' He remains busy outside a team role: doing TV commentary work, appearing regularly on The Red Flags Podcast, and holding a stake in the Red Bull-backed Tech3 MotoGP squad. He gave no indication of a specific team or timeline for any return.
key_points: Former Haas team boss **Guenther Steiner**, ousted in **January 2024**, says he's open to an F1 return.
His condition: it has to be **'a project I like'** — something he can shape himself, not just a job title.
He's currently a TV pundit and holds an **ownership stake in the Red Bull KTM Tech3 MotoGP team**.
Steiner became a fan-favourite worldwide through his blunt, funny appearances on Netflix's **Drive to Survive**.

depth.background: Guenther Steiner ran the Haas F1 team from its founding in 2016 until the team fired him in **January 2024**, despite him having turned the small American outfit into one of the sport's most recognizable personalities via Netflix's Drive to Survive documentary series. Since leaving Haas, he's stayed close to motorsport as a television pundit and taken an ownership stake in the Tech3 MotoGP team backed by Red Bull, but hasn't held another team-principal role in F1.

stories.title: Trump's press secretary Karoline Leavitt is resigning at the end of August, to become a top campaign advisor
stories.what_happened: President Trump announced on **Wednesday, August 12** that Karoline Leavitt will leave her post as White House press secretary by the end of the month. Leavitt, 28, had returned to the podium only weeks earlier after parental leave for the birth of her second child in **May**. Trump said she is leaving **"so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family, a decision I totally understand and respect,"** and that she will instead become **one of his top outside advisors**, working with the Republican Party to help win the **November midterm elections**. Trump did not name a successor. Reporting has floated **Katie Miller** (wife of aide Stephen Miller, herself a former administration communications official) and Fox News host **Kari Lake** as possible replacements, though nothing is confirmed.
key_points: Karoline Leavitt, at **28** the youngest White House press secretary in history, is stepping down by **end of August**.
Trump says she'll become one of his **"top outside advisors"** ahead of the **November midterms**.
She had only recently returned from **parental leave** after the birth of her second child in May.
The prior record for youngest press secretary belonged to Ronald Ziegler, who was **29** under Nixon in 1969.
No successor has been named; reported contenders include **Katie Miller** and Fox host **Kari Lake**.

depth.background: The White House press secretary is the administration's daily public voice — the person who stands at the podium and takes reporters' questions on the record, shaping how the government's actions get explained to the public. Leavitt became the youngest person ever to hold the job when Trump named her to it in **November 2024**, ahead of his second term. She has been a close, combative defender of the administration's messaging since, making her departure notable well beyond a routine staff change.

stories.title: Red Bull sweetens its offer to Verstappen with a 5-year deal to 2033 — but he reportedly wants just one year instead
stories.what_happened: According to multiple reports, Red Bull has revised its contract offer to Verstappen from the previously reported $80 million-a-year, 2029-end deal to a longer **five-year contract running to the end of 2033**. Verstappen, however, reportedly wants the opposite: an **alternative one-year contract** that would let him evaluate whether Red Bull can build him a genuinely winning car for the **2027** rules reset before committing to anything longer. His exit clause remains live, and he has until **October** to formally decide whether to invoke it and leave.
key_points: Red Bull has revised its offer to Verstappen to a **five-year deal** running to the end of **2033**.
Verstappen reportedly wants the opposite: a **one-year contract** to test Red Bull's 2027 car before committing long-term.
His **exit clause** is active because he ended the summer break outside the championship's **top two**.
He must tell Red Bull by **October** whether he intends to leave.
Red Bull's **RB22** has been the slowest of the top four cars this season, with **zero race wins**.

depth.background: Max Verstappen is a **four-time world champion** who has raced for Red Bull his entire F1 career, but the team has struggled badly under 2026's new hybrid engine rules — its RB22 has been the slowest of the top four cars all season without a single win. His current contract runs to 2028 but contains **performance-linked exit clauses**; because Red Bull fell out of the championship's top two by the summer break, one of those clauses activated, giving Verstappen the option to leave early. Negotiations over a new deal have been ongoing since.

thread.previously: We reported Red Bull had tabled a new contract worth about $80 million a season, running to the end of 2029 and deleting Verstappen's exit clause, with his camp given until October to decide.
thread.changed: Red Bull has now revised that offer to a longer five-year deal running to the end of 2033, but Verstappen reportedly wants the opposite — a shorter one-year contract instead, so he can judge whether Red Bull can actually build him a winning car for 2027 before committing further.

stories.title: Colombia's 72-hour rescue window closes as the toll passes 220 and aid refusals spark backlash
stories.what_happened: As the **72-hour survival window** narrowed and then closed, Colombia's government confirmed it had initially declined most international rescue offers, requesting help from only the **US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel** and stating it would rely on national rescuers instead — a marked contrast to how neighboring Venezuela accepted dozens of foreign teams without question after its own recent quakes. Colombian forensic authorities separately put the death toll at **more than 227**, above the government's own running count, while roughly **195 people remain officially listed as missing** — though volunteer-run databases estimate the real number closer to **4,000**, reflecting how hard it is to get an accurate count with damaged phone networks and blocked roads. Peru has now confirmed it will dispatch volunteers to help. Colombia's disaster-management chief defended the limited outside help, denying any ideological motive behind the decision.
key_points: The critical **72-hour survival window** for finding people alive in rubble has effectively closed, four days after the quake.
Colombia initially **limited foreign rescue offers to just four countries**, relying mainly on domestic teams — a choice now under public criticism.
Forensic authorities put the death toll at **over 227**, higher than the government's own count, with the true figure still likely rising.
**Peru** has now confirmed it will send volunteers, after Colombia widened its request for outside help.
This is being called the **first major controversy** of new president Abelardo de la Espriella's government.

depth.background: A **magnitude-7.4 earthquake** struck western Colombia's coffee-growing region on Sunday, August 9, and is the country's deadliest in decades. It leveled buildings across Chocó and hit hardest in Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdó, with roads into the epicenter near San José del Palmar blocked by landslides for days. The disaster landed just days into the term of Colombia's new hard-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, making it the first major crisis test of his administration.

thread.previously: We reported the confirmed death toll had risen to at least 224, with 700 injured and roughly 5,000 homes damaged or destroyed; Colombia's newly inaugurated president gave the first full damage briefing, and a woman was pulled alive from rubble after 30 hours.
thread.changed: The critical **72-hour survival window** — the point after which the odds of finding people alive in collapsed buildings drop sharply — has now effectively closed. It has also emerged that Colombia's government initially turned away most foreign rescue offers, asking for help from only four countries (the US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel) and citing sole reliance on domestic rescuers — a decision now drawing criticism as the young government's first real crisis controversy.

stories.title: Red Bull tables an $80 million-a-year offer to erase Verstappen's exit clause and keep him to 2029
stories.what_happened: With Verstappen technically free to negotiate elsewhere, Red Bull has moved to keep him by tabling a new contract reportedly worth around **$80 million per season** — a significant raise on his current roughly €65 million annual pay — that would extend his stay to the end of **2029** and delete the exit clause altogether. According to multiple reports, Verstappen's camp has so far **not signed**, and has been given until **October** to decide. Former Dutch F1 driver Robert Doornbos has suggested Verstappen could confirm his decision at the upcoming **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort** — the circuit's final F1 race for the foreseeable future — given the sentimental timing and the limited realistic alternatives elsewhere on the grid.
key_points: Red Bull's new offer is reportedly worth around **$80 million a season**, up from roughly €65 million currently.
The deal would extend Verstappen's stay to the end of **2029** and **remove the exit clause** that made him a free agent this week.
Verstappen's management has **not yet accepted**, with reports of an **October deadline** to decide.
Speculation is building that Verstappen could **announce his decision at Zandvoort**, the season's next race and the final-ever Dutch Grand Prix at that circuit.
Mercedes and McLaren remain the two teams seen as realistic alternatives if he leaves, though McLaren has said it's happy with its current lineup.

depth.background: Verstappen's existing Red Bull contract runs through 2028 but contains a performance clause: if he fell outside the top two in the championship entering the summer break, he could walk away without breaching the deal. That clause activated on August 11, turning the four-time world champion into F1's most sought-after free agent just as Red Bull's car, the RB22, has struggled to keep pace with Mercedes and McLaren this season.

thread.previously: We reported that Verstappen's Red Bull contract contains a performance-based exit clause that had formally activated because he entered the summer break outside the top two in the drivers' championship — making him, in practical terms, a free agent that rival teams like Mercedes and McLaren could legally approach.
thread.changed: Red Bull has now responded with a concrete counter-offer: a new contract worth roughly **$80 million a season** — well above his current pay — that would keep Verstappen at the team through **2029** and remove the exit clause entirely. Verstappen's camp has reportedly not yet accepted, sitting on the offer with an **October deadline** to decide.

stories.title: An overloaded ferry capsizes on Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba, killing at least 44
stories.what_happened: A government passenger ferry that runs between the town of Kariba and surrounding islands and fishing villages capsized in choppy conditions, killing at least **44 people** so far, with search and rescue operations still ongoing for dozens more who remain missing. The vessel's rated capacity was 90 people, but it was carrying at least **114 adult passengers** plus 5 crew members and an unknown number of children when it went down — meaning it was significantly overloaded. A survivor told Zimbabwe's national broadcaster, ZBC, that passengers had pleaded with the ferry operator to turn back once the water got rough, but he refused to do so. Authorities have deployed a specialized aquatic rescue unit by air to the area, and two funeral parlors have been engaged to handle recovery of the dead.
key_points: At least **44 people have drowned** after a passenger ferry capsized on Lake Kariba, with dozens still missing.
The boat's official capacity was **90 people** — it was carrying **114 adult passengers**, 5 crew, and an unspecified number of children.
A survivor says passengers **begged the driver to turn back** because of choppy water, but he refused.
Lake Kariba is the **world's largest man-made lake** and a vital transport link for islands and fishing villages with no roads.
A specialized aquatic rescue unit was **airlifted in** to search for survivors and recover bodies.

depth.background: Lake Kariba, formed by a dam on the Zambezi River, is the largest artificial lake in the world by volume, and it sits between Zimbabwe and Zambia. Because many communities on its shores and islands have no road access, government-run ferries are often the only practical way for people to travel, trade, and reach markets or hospitals. That reliance on a handful of aging vessels is exactly why overcrowding is a chronic risk on routes like this one.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake toll climbs as rescuers race the 72-hour survival window
stories.what_happened: The quake leveled homes across Chocó, and the official death toll — verified case by case by Colombian authorities — stands at **181**, with **2,595 people injured**. Officials list **195 more as missing**, but volunteer networks tracking family reports separately estimate the true number of unaccounted-for people is closer to **4,000**, reflecting how hard it is to get an accurate count in a disaster zone with damaged phone networks and blocked roads. Search-and-rescue teams are now in a race against the **72-hour mark** since the quake struck — the rough threshold after which the odds of finding people alive in collapsed buildings drop off sharply. Rescuers still haven't been able to physically reach the epicenter near San José del Palmar because access roads are damaged or blocked by landslides.
key_points: Colombian officials confirm **at least 181 dead** and **2,595 injured** as of Wednesday's count, two days after the quake.
**195 people are officially missing**, but volunteer-run databases put the real number closer to **4,000**.
Rescue teams are racing the **72-hour survival window** — the point after which chances of finding survivors in rubble fall steeply.
Roads into the epicenter near **San José del Palmar** remain blocked, so some of the worst-hit areas still haven't been reached.
The disaster is the first major crisis test for Colombia's new president, **Abelardo de la Espriella**.

depth.background: A magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck Colombia's mountainous Chocó department on Monday, August 10, one of the strongest quakes to hit the country in decades. The region is remote and poorly connected, which is why it has taken days for rescue teams and even accurate casualty counts to reach the outside world. Colombia's government changed hands earlier this year, and this is the **first major natural disaster** the new administration has had to manage.

thread.previously: We reported the magnitude-7.4 quake that hit Colombia's Chocó department had killed more than 220 people, with President Abelardo de la Espriella saying at least 5,000 homes were destroyed.
thread.changed: Colombian authorities now confirm at least 181 dead and 2,595 injured as the official count is re-verified, with 195 more listed as missing officially — though civilian-run databases put that figure closer to 4,000. Search teams are racing against the 72-hour mark after which survival chances in collapsed buildings drop sharply, and rescuers still can't reach the epicenter near San José del Palmar.

stories.title: Cadillac fires its first-ever F1 team boss, Graeme Lowdon, a week before the season resumes
stories.what_happened: Cadillac fired Graeme Lowdon as team principal and immediately named **Marcin Budkowski** as his replacement, in what the team is calling a 'planned leadership transition as the organization evolves from its initial build phase into the next stage of racing performance.' The change was announced on **Wednesday, August 12**, just a week before the F1 season resumes at the Dutch Grand Prix following the summer break. Cadillac CEO **Dan Towriss** said the call was his alone and that Lowdon was informed only that Wednesday morning, though the two had previously discussed that some kind of transition would eventually happen. Budkowski, 49, brings experience from stints at Ferrari, McLaren and the FIA, and most recently served as an executive director at Alpine until 2022. The timing is notable: Cadillac remains the only team on the 2026 grid that hasn't scored a championship point through the season's first 11 rounds.
key_points: Cadillac has **sacked team principal Graeme Lowdon**, replacing him with **Marcin Budkowski**.
The move comes just **a week before F1 resumes** with the Dutch Grand Prix, and lands mid-season.
Cadillac is F1's newest team, backed by **General Motors**, and is the **only team yet to score a point** through 11 rounds of 2026.
Budkowski, 49, previously worked at **Ferrari, McLaren, and the FIA**, and was most recently an Alpine director.
Cadillac's CEO says the decision was **his alone**, and Lowdon was only told on the morning it happened.

depth.background: Cadillac, backed by General Motors and TWG Motorsports, joined the Formula 1 grid in 2026 as the sport's newest team, signing experienced drivers Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Pérez to lead its debut season. Graeme Lowdon was the team's first-ever principal, tasked with building the outfit from scratch. Starting a brand-new F1 team is notoriously difficult — new entrants typically need several seasons before they're competitive against established rivals with years of infrastructure and know-how already in place.

stories.title: Researchers find a flaw that let weaker AI models leak stronger models' hidden reasoning — and even passwords
stories.what_happened: The researchers found that an encrypted reasoning block created in one session could be **replayed into a different session** and, if handed to a **cheaper, lighter model from the same company**, would sometimes get decoded and printed out in plain text — because lighter models are built with less aggressive filtering than a company's flagship model. Testing this against thousands of publicly logged AI-agent conversations, the team recovered **over 315,000 hidden reasoning blocks**, some of which contained sensitive data like API keys and passwords that had leaked into a model's internal reasoning. The three companies have since updated how they handle this: **Anthropic** now says reasoning blocks are tied to the specific model that created them and should be discarded when switching models; **Google** says its backend manages compatibility automatically; **OpenAI** still instructs developers to replay reasoning blocks manually.
key_points: Security researchers showed **OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google's** AI systems could be tricked into revealing their **encrypted internal "reasoning"** — normally hidden from users.
The trick: replaying a hidden-reasoning block from one session into **a weaker model** in the same family, which lacks the safety filtering to refuse and just prints it out.
Across **6,708 public AI-agent conversation logs**, researchers decoded **315,320 hidden reasoning blocks**, some containing **leaked API keys and passwords**.

The flaw enables **four types of abuse**: stealing reasoning to copy a rival's model, extracting private user data, uncovering content models were told to hide, and smuggling hidden instructions past safety checks.

depth.background: Modern AI "reasoning" models think through a problem in a hidden scratchpad before giving their final answer — a technique that improves accuracy but that companies keep encrypted and invisible to protect their trade secrets and prevent misuse. Developers who build tools on top of these models sometimes need to pass that hidden reasoning between separate API calls to keep a conversation coherent, which is where this flaw lived. A research team published a paper titled "Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs" documenting how they exploited this.

stories.title: US-Iran talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz break down, and oil prices rise on the deadlock
stories.what_happened: Iran told mediators that a technical agreement with Oman on strait management **would not be enough on its own** — Tehran is now also demanding the US ease sanctions and pay war reparations before it will let normal shipping resume. Talks stalled as a result, and **oil prices rose** on the fading odds of a quick resolution: Brent crude settled near **$89 a barrel** and US crude (WTI) near **$83**. Iran's Supreme Leader Khamenei's son and de facto successor, Mojtaba Khamenei, named a new military high command, including Ali Abdollahi as armed forces chief of staff. Trump reiterated that the US would not tolerate interference with shipping, while Gulf states have grown visibly frustrated at being caught between the two sides.
key_points: Oil prices climbed after **Iran added new demands** — including eased US sanctions and **war reparations** — before it will reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

The strait normally carries about **one-fifth of the world's oil supply**; shipping through it has collapsed to **8–15 vessels crossing on Aug 4–6**, versus roughly **130 transits before the conflict**.
Iran's Supreme Leader reshuffled the country's **top military leadership**, naming new armed forces and Revolutionary Guard commanders.
President Trump said the US has **"total control"** of the strait and warned Iran would **"get blown away"** if it interfered with shipping there.

depth.background: Since a US-Israel-Iran war erupted in late February 2026, Iranian attacks on shipping and US retaliatory strikes have repeatedly disrupted the **Strait of Hormuz**, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that oil tankers must pass through to leave the Gulf. Periodic ceasefire efforts and partial truces have not held, and Trump has followed a pattern of threatening major new strikes and then pulling back. Earlier in August, Iran appeared close to a deal with Oman on managing traffic through the strait, which briefly lifted hopes of it reopening.

thread.previously: Yesterday's coverage focused on the rupee and Indian oil companies bleeding money as the strait stayed shut, with a deal seen as unlikely soon.
thread.changed: Today the block is explicitly on the diplomatic track: Iran has added new demands (sanctions relief, reparations) that talks with Oman alone can't satisfy, oil prices have ticked up in response, and Iran has also reshuffled its military command.

stories.title: Tata Sons begins the search for its next chairman — and its own 2022 rules make the obvious successor ineligible
stories.what_happened: Chandrasekaran's resignation, confirmed yesterday, means Tata Sons must now run its succession process for the first time since 2017, under a formal mechanism written into the company's **Articles of Association**. Because Tata Trusts hold the controlling stake in Tata Sons, they get the decisive say in who becomes the next chairman. That creates an immediate complication: **Noel Tata**, seen as the natural internal candidate given his family ties and current seniority, already chairs Tata Trusts — and the 2022 provision that split the two roles means he cannot simply take the Tata Sons chairmanship too without stepping back from the Trusts, or the rule being changed. The group's AGM is scheduled for **August 18**, just days away, without a new chairman named.
key_points: Tata Sons' succession process is now formally underway after **N. Chandrasekaran's** resignation, with a **formal Articles-of-Association mechanism** to follow.
**Tata Trusts**, which hold the majority stake in Tata Sons, will play the **key role** in picking the next chairman.
**Noel Tata**, the most obvious internal candidate, currently chairs Tata Trusts — and a **2022 rule bars one person from leading both** the Trusts and Tata Sons at once.
The group's **AGM on August 18** goes ahead without a confirmed successor in place, leaving Tata effectively **leaderless** at the top in the interim.

depth.background: Tata Sons is the holding company that controls the sprawling Tata Group — from Tata Motors and Tata Steel to TCS and Air India — making its chairman one of the most powerful roles in Indian business. Ratan Tata led the group for decades before handing over to Cyrus Mistry, whose abrupt removal in 2016 triggered a bitter public and legal fight; Chandrasekaran took over in 2017 to restore stability. In 2022, the Tata Trusts' rules were changed to formally separate the Trusts' leadership from the Tata Sons chairmanship, partly to prevent any one person concentrating that much power again.

thread.previously: Yesterday's coverage was about the resignation itself — Chandrasekaran stepping down after Noel Tata blocked his reappointment over concerns about weak financial performance at some Tata companies.
thread.changed: Today's news is about what happens next: the formal succession process has begun, and it has run into an unexpected snag — the Tata Trusts/Tata Sons dual-role rule the group itself adopted in 2022 rules out the most obvious successor, Noel Tata, unless something changes before the August 18 AGM.

stories.title: George Russell says he's talked to a sports psychologist every week for six years to handle F1 pressure
stories.what_happened: In a new interview, **George Russell** said he has worked with a **sports psychologist on a weekly basis for six years**, describing it as something he does **'not necessarily for tough times'** but as an ongoing part of how he manages a Formula 1 season. He traced the habit back to a **difficult period earlier in his career** that pushed him to seek professional support for the first time, and said he quickly recognized the benefit and kept it up. Russell said the sessions now help him manage **pressure, energy levels and self-belief** across a full season rather than just around specific difficult races. The comments arrive mid-way through a tight **2026 title fight**, in which Russell sits third in the standings behind Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.
key_points: Mercedes driver **George Russell** revealed he has spoken to a **sports psychologist every week for six years**, not just during tough moments.
Russell said the sessions began after a **low point early in his career** and have become routine for managing the **pressure, energy and performance** demands of a full F1 season.
He described using the sessions **proactively** rather than only in crisis — a shift he says reflects how his own view of mental health has evolved over the past two years.
The comments come as Russell fights for the **2026 drivers' championship**, currently sitting **third**, behind teammate **Kimi Antonelli** and Ferrari's **Lewis Hamilton**.

depth.background: Formula 1 is one of the most mentally demanding sports in the world — drivers make split-second decisions above 300 km/h while managing intense media scrutiny, sponsor obligations and, for title contenders, season-long championship pressure. Mental health has become a more openly discussed topic in F1 over the past several years, with drivers including Russell speaking publicly about anxiety, burnout and therapy — a shift from a sport that historically prized a tough, stoic image. Russell has touched on this before, but this interview goes further, framing psychological support as a routine performance tool rather than a response to crisis.

stories.title: India's rupee slides to fresh lows and oil firms bleed ₹1,000 crore a day as the Strait of Hormuz standoff drags on
stories.what_happened: On **Wednesday, August 12**, the rupee weakened further to **95.42 against the dollar** in early trade, extending a run of record lows, as Brent crude climbed back toward **$90 a barrel** after hopes faded for a quick US-Iran deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Oil marketing companies are now losing up to **₹1,000 crore (roughly $115 million) a day**, since they sell fuel at government-capped prices well below what it now costs them to import crude. India has lost more than **40% of its normal crude flows** since the strait closed, forcing it to source oil from costlier alternative routes. Compounding the pressure, foreign investors have pulled more than **$20 billion** out of Indian equities in the first four months of 2026, and analysts now expect India's GDP growth to slow to **6.7%** in FY2026-27, down from 7.7% the year before.
key_points: Rupee fell to **95.42 per dollar**, extending a slide to record lows
Brent crude pushed toward **$90 a barrel** on fading hopes of a quick Hormuz reopening
India has lost over **40% of its crude oil flows** since the Strait of Hormuz closed
State oil marketing companies are bleeding up to **₹1,000 crore a day** to keep pump prices low
Foreign investors have pulled more than **$20 billion** from Indian stocks this year

depth.background: India imports roughly **85% of the crude oil** it consumes, and a large share historically transits the **Strait of Hormuz**, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which about a fifth of the world's oil normally flows. Tensions from the **2026 Iran war**, which began in February, have periodically closed or restricted the strait, forcing India to scramble for alternative crude sources and squeezing its trade balance. The government has kept retail petrol and diesel prices largely frozen through the crisis to shield consumers, meaning the losses instead land on state-owned oil marketing companies.

stories.title: Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran resigns after a board member blocks his reappointment, leaving India's biggest conglomerate without a clear successor
stories.what_happened: Chandrasekaran announced on **August 12**, days before Tata Sons' Annual General Meeting, that he will step down as chairman and will **not seek reappointment** — but will complete his current term, which runs until **February 2027**, giving the group time to find a successor. In his statement, he said **'one of the board members did not support'** the proposal to extend his tenure, and in the absence of unanimous backing, he chose to defer the decision rather than push it through. He has asked the Tata Sons board to begin a formal succession process **immediately**. The announcement threw the country's largest conglomerate — spanning steel, cars, IT services, and airlines — into a period of leadership uncertainty.
key_points: Chandrasekaran will **not seek reappointment** when his term ends in **February 2027**
The move follows **one board member refusing to support** extending his tenure
He has asked the board to **start a formal succession process** immediately
Tata Group stocks came under **heavy selling pressure**, dragging the Sensex lower
He has steered Tata through its post-Ratan Tata transition since **2017**

depth.background: **N. Chandrasekaran** ('Chandra') has run **Tata Sons**, the holding company that controls the sprawling Tata Group — Tata Motors, Tata Steel, Tata Consultancy Services, Air India, and dozens more — since **2017**, when he became the group's first chairman from outside the Tata family. Under him, Tata expanded into semiconductors and electric vehicles, and reacquired **Air India** from the government in 2022. His term was due for renewal, a decision that under Tata Sons' governance culture is expected to have board consensus rather than pass on a simple majority.

stories.title: The Hundred's last league day sets up the Eliminators, with Trent Rockets already through to Lord's final

The last qualification place came down to Wednesday's fixtures, including **Welsh Fire vs London Spirit** at Sophia Gardens and **Birmingham Phoenix vs MI London** at Edgbaston, with the third-place finisher joining Manchester Super Giants in the men's **Eliminator at The Kia Oval on August 14**. **Manchester Super Giants** have booked the other men's Eliminator spot
Wednesday's deciders include **Welsh Fire vs London Spirit** and **Birmingham Phoenix vs MI London**

stories.title: Australia reunite Cummins-Starc-Hazlewood pace attack for first Bangladesh Test, as hosts wait on Shanto's XI amid camp 'niggles'

Australia, meanwhile, are using this series to open a **20-Test year** that will also include tours of South Africa, India, and England, as part of the ongoing World Test Championship cycle.

stories.title: India's defence spokesperson calls Chinese troop reports near Arunachal 'unsubstantiated', as MEA holds firm line
stories.what_happened: A day after India's Ministry of External Affairs first responded to unverified reports of Chinese troop activity near Arunachal Pradesh, more specific details have emerged: the reported face-off site is **Taksing**, in the Upper Subhansiri district, about **2.5km inside** territory controlled by India. Reports say Chinese troops initially withdrew from the area but returned in early August and pitched a couple of tents. MEA spokesperson **Randhir Jaiswal** reiterated that India considers the state of the border 'most serious' and that it 'will define' the wider relationship with Beijing. But an **Indian defence spokesperson** pushed back harder than the government had so far, calling the reports **'unsubstantiated and uncorroborated, without any verification'**. The mixed messaging — a pointed MEA warning alongside a defence-side denial — continues even as the two sides work to keep ties on a stabilizing track ahead of September's BRICS summit in Delhi.
key_points: India's foreign ministry says **border peace is critical** to its relationship with China, per spokesperson **Randhir Jaiswal**.
The reported face-off site is **Taksing**, in the Upper Subhansiri district of Arunachal Pradesh, **2.5km inside** Indian-controlled territory.
Chinese troops reportedly **withdrew, then returned in early August** and pitched tents at the site.
An **Indian defence spokesperson** has now directly called the reports **'unsubstantiated and uncorroborated'** — a sharper denial than before.
It comes ahead of a **BRICS summit in New Delhi** (September 12-13) that China's Xi Jinping is expected to attend.

depth.background: India and China share a long, disputed frontier called the **Line of Actual Control (LAC)**, which has never been formally demarcated. Arunachal Pradesh, an Indian state China claims in full as 'South Tibet', has repeatedly been a flashpoint. The two countries have been cautiously rebuilding ties since a deadly 2020 clash in the Galwan Valley, including a resumed round of border talks on August 6 — which is the backdrop against which these fresh troop-movement reports surfaced.

stories.title: Godrej Consumer shares sink 10% after CEO Sudhir Sitapati's sudden resignation

stories.title: A record 231-run stand powers Afghanistan to a series-sealing 42-run win over Ireland
stories.what_happened: Afghanistan posted a commanding **343 for 9** in the 4th ODI at Belfast's Civil Service Cricket Club, anchored by a **231-run partnership** between **Ibrahim Zadran** and **Sediqullah Atal** — the highest second-wicket stand in Afghanistan's ODI history. Afghanistan's bowlers, led by **Yamin Ahmadzai (4 for 71)** and spin great **Rashid Khan (3 for 49)**, closed out the win. The result gives Afghanistan an **unassailable 3-0 lead** in the five-match series, with the fifth and final ODI still to come.

**Ibrahim Zadran and Sediqullah Atal put on 231 runs** together — Afghanistan's highest-ever 2nd-wicket stand in ODIs.
**Sediqullah Atal scored 143** off 120 balls and was named Player of the Match.

stories.title: BCCI scraps the A+ grade and demotes Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli to Grade B in new central contracts
stories.what_happened: The BCCI finalized its central contracts for the **2026-27 season**, and the changes were significant: the **A+ grade has been scrapped altogether**, and the new top Grade A now includes just **three players** — captain-calibre all-rounder Ravindra Jadeja, fast bowler Jasprit Bumrah, and India's Test and ODI captain Shubman Gill. key_points: The BCCI's **A+ category, its top tier since 2018**, has been scrapped entirely.
Only **three players** — Shubman Gill, Jasprit Bumrah, and Ravindra Jadeja — now hold the new top Grade A.
**Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli have been demoted** from A+ to Grade B.
